181	 Introduction
182	
183	       Though there is no universally accepted definition of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI),
184	
185	it is generally defined as an acute brain injury resulting from mechanical energy to the head from
186	
187	external physical forces1, 2. Diagnostic criteria include loss of consciousness less than 30
188	
189	minutes, post traumatic amnesia less than 24 hours, a Glascow Coma Scale score of 13 to 152, as
190	
191	well as mental status and behavioral changes, and/or neurological signs 3. Though the clinical
192	
193	
194	                                                                           D
195	presentation of mTBI can vary, often the terms mTBI and concussion are used interchangeably3.
196	
197	Of particular interest in the athletic population is sport-related concussion (SRC). SRC is defined
198	
199	
200	
201	
202	                           EP
203	as brain injury resulting in the disturbance of typical brain functioning and involves a complex
204	
205	pathophysiological process4-6. SRC incidence is estimated to be around 3.8 million injuries per
206	
207	
208	
209	
210	                             TE
211	year in the United States7. At the high-school level, the incidence rate of SRCs is highest in
212	
213	boys’ football (10.40 per 10,000 athletic exposures [AEs]), followed by girls’ soccer (8.19 per
214	
215	10,000 AEs) and boys’ ice hockey (7.69 per 10,000 AEs)8. SRCs can also occur at all levels of
216	
217	low contact sports (e.g. tennis, swimming, track and field). The true incidence of SRC is likely
218	
219	higher than documented, as many athletes may not recognize or report their SRC9-11. Notably,
220	
221	             C
222	the Center for Disease Control and Prevention claims that five out of ten concussions go
223	
224	undiagnosed or undetected12.
225	
226	 C
227	A      The biomechanical forces involved in concussion include direct impact to the head, or an
228	
229	impact to another part of the body with a mechanical force transmitted to the head13. These
230	
231	forces can be linear or rotational14. In addition to increased acceleration, the direction of
232	
233	acceleration is also important, as head impacts in the real world occur in all planes of motion.
234	
235	There is evidence to suggest that coronal plane acceleration (lateral flexion) may be more
236	
237	
238	
239	
240	                                                        4
241	
242	       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
243	 injurious than sagittal plane acceleration (flexion and extension)15. Ultimately, a better
244	
245	understanding of the biomechanical forces that cause concussion may lead to more targeted
246	
247	prevention approaches.
248	
249	
250	
251	       Although the medical community’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat SRC has greatly
252	
253	improved, the ability to prevent SRCs from occurring and decrease the severity of clinical
254	
255	
256	                                                                           D
257	outcomes post-injury is limited16. If the acceleration of the brain during an impact can be
258	
259	decreased14, it has been theorized that this could prevent a concussion from occurring. This is an
260	
261	
262	
263	
264	                           EP
265	important concept as the greatest opportunity to impact overall injury burden often lies in injury
266	
267	prevention14. However, the literature is sparse in regard to concussion prevention in athletes.
268	
269	
270	
271	
272	                             TE
273	Patricios et al. has recently published a revised consensus statement on concussion in sport.
274	
275	While there were five unanimously-supported recommendations for concussion prevention (i:
276	
277	Mouthguard use should be supported in child and adolescent ice hockey, ii: Policy disallowing
278	
279	body checking should be supported for all children and most levels of adolescent ice hockey, iii:
280	
281	Strategies limiting contact practice in American football should inform related policies and
282	
283	             C
284	recommendations for all levels, iv: neuromuscular training warm-up programmes are
285	
286	
287	
288	 C
289	recommended, based on research in rugby, and more research is needed for female athletes and
290	
291	in other team sports specifically targeting exercise components aimed to reduce concussion rates,
292	
293	
294	
295	A
296	v: Policy supporting optimal concussion management strategies to reduce recurrent concussion
297	
298	rates is recommended)17, none of the recommendations included cervical strength. Four of the
299	
300	recommendations were specific to a singular sport and the fifth was a general comment about
301	
302	policy change17. Thus, there are no agreed upon guidelines or formal recommendations in regard
303	
304	to cervical strength or cervical strengthening programs and athlete concussion reduction.
305	
306	
307	
308	
309	                                                        5
310	
311	       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
312	        Neck size and neck strength have emerged as modifiable characteristics associated with
313	
314	concussion risk12, 14. Neck size is an easily measured variable given that neck circumference can
315	
316	be obtained with simple and accessible tools, like a measuring tape. Isometric neck strength,
317	
318	though a more difficult variable to test due to the need for equipment, such as a dynamometer,
319	
320	may be more clinically useful because it is a more functional characteristic as opposed to neck
321	
322	size alone, which is static measurement. There also may be certain athlete populations that could
323	
324	
325	                                                                           D
326	benefit from a formal cervical strengthening program, since they have weaker necks18, 19,
327	
328	including amateur athletes and female athletes. Due to the paucity of research and data on this
329	
330	
331	
332	
333	                           EP
334	topic, the purpose of this narrative review is to examine all the literature available regarding neck
335	
336	size and/or neck strength and its relation to SRC prevention and if a formal cervical strength
337	
338	
339	
340	
341	                             TE
342	training program decreases SRCs.
343	
344	
345	
346	Methods
347	
348	       A search of Ovid MEDLINE database was performed with the key terms outlined in box
349	
350	A, resulting in 13 articles. Google Scholar was utilized to search for additional articles with key
351	
352	             C
353	terms outlined in box B, resulting in 552 articles. An additional filter to exclude articles prior to
354	
355	
356	
357	  C
358	the year 2000 was used, which resulted in 485 articles. As there is a paucity of research in this
359	
360	area spread across a variety of sports and athlete populations, the inclusion criteria was
361	
362	
363	
364	A
365	intentionally kept broad to ensure we captured the literature available on the topic. All articles
366	
367	relating to sports related concussion and neck size and/or neck strength were included, regardless
368	
369	of the sport, gender of the athletes, or age of the athletes. The primary author reviewed the
370	
371	remaining 485 articles and included all 22 articles related to sports related concussion. Two
372	
373	articles were later removed during the article revision process as they were outside the scope of
374	
375	
376	
377	
378	                                                        6

381	 this manuscript. Combining the 20 articles from Google Scholar and 13 articles from Ovid
382	
383	MEDLINE resulted in a total of 33 articles included for this literature review (Figure 1).
384	
385	
386	
387	Discussion
388	
389	Neck Size
390	
391	       Neck size, typically measured as neck circumference, was theorized to be a protective
392	
393	
394	                                                                           D
395	factor for concussion, as a larger neck could mechanically resist more force and prevent a
396	
397	concussion from occurring. Neck circumference has been proposed as a simple proxy measure of
398	
399	
400	
401	
402	                           EP
403	other features of the cervical spine, such as neck strength20. However, the literature does not
404	
405	support this theory. Neck circumference has not been shown to be related to SRC history or
406	
407	
408	
409	
410	                             TE
411	subsequent SRC. Since neck size is not related to SRC, additional studies examined proportional
412	
413	neck circumference (neck circumference in proportion to body mass)20. Similarly, there was no
414	
415	relationship to proportional neck circumference and reduction of SRC. Males had a significantly
416	
417	larger neck circumference and proportional neck circumference compared to females, but when
418	
419	controlling for sex, there was no association between neck circumference and SRC20. Eckner et
420	
421	             C
422	al. found possible evidence that increased neck size may correlate with reduced concussion risk
423	
424	in high-school aged male athletes involved in contact or collision sports21. Their results showed

     Risk Reduction of Concussion in Athletes: Do Neck Size or Neck Strength

                                                 Make a Difference?




     Sean Silverman, DO1, Meghan E. Vidt, PhD1,2, Justin S. Hong, MD1, Lori M. Grafton, MD1

 Abstract

Medical provider’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat sport-related concussion (SRC) has

greatly improved in recent years. Though more is known about the biomechanical forces

involved in concussion, it is still uncertain whether there are preventative measures athletes can

take to prevent a SRC from occurring. The objective of this review was to determine if either

neck size or neck strength is related to a decreased risk of sustaining a SRC. A literature review


                                                                           D
was conducted on Google Scholar and Ovid MEDLINE for pertinent articles. Findings indicate

that isometric neck strength, but not neck size, has been shown to be a predictor for SRC




                           EP
prevention. Formal neck strengthening programs are feasible and lead to decreased SRC risk.

Additionally, there may be greater opportunity to increase neck strength in amateur athletes




                             TE
compared to professional. In conclusion, cervical strengthening programs have been shown to be

feasible and beneficial for athletes to decrease their risk of sustaining a SRC, though the optimal

duration, intensity, and frequency has yet to be determined.



Keywords: brain concussion, concussion, primary prevention, neck strengthening, cervical

strengtheningC
 C
List of Abbreviations

mTBI, Mild Traumatic Brain Injury



A
SRC, Sport-related concussion

AE, athletic exposure

U18, under age 18

FIFA 11 +, Federation Internationale de Football Association’s 11+ Injury Prevention Program




                                                        3

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Introduction

       Though there is no universally accepted definition of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI),

it is generally defined as an acute brain injury resulting from mechanical energy to the head from

external physical forces1, 2. Diagnostic criteria include loss of consciousness less than 30

minutes, post traumatic amnesia less than 24 hours, a Glascow Coma Scale score of 13 to 152, as

well as mental status and behavioral changes, and/or neurological signs 3. Though the clinical


                                                                           D
presentation of mTBI can vary, often the terms mTBI and concussion are used interchangeably3.

Of particular interest in the athletic population is sport-related concussion (SRC). SRC is defined




                           EP
as brain injury resulting in the disturbance of typical brain functioning and involves a complex

pathophysiological process4-6. SRC incidence is estimated to be around 3.8 million injuries per




                             TE
year in the United States7. At the high-school level, the incidence rate of SRCs is highest in

boys’ football (10.40 per 10,000 athletic exposures [AEs]), followed by girls’ soccer (8.19 per

10,000 AEs) and boys’ ice hockey (7.69 per 10,000 AEs)8. SRCs can also occur at all levels of

low contact sports (e.g. tennis, swimming, track and field). The true incidence of SRC is likely

higher than documented, as many athletes may not recognize or report their SRC9-11. Notably,

             C
the Center for Disease Control and Prevention claims that five out of ten concussions go

undiagnosed or undetected12.

 C
A      The biomechanical forces involved in concussion include direct impact to the head, or an

impact to another part of the body with a mechanical force transmitted to the head13. These

forces can be linear or rotational14. In addition to increased acceleration, the direction of

acceleration is also important, as head impacts in the real world occur in all planes of motion.

There is evidence to suggest that coronal plane acceleration (lateral flexion) may be more




                                                        4

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 injurious than sagittal plane acceleration (flexion and extension)15. Ultimately, a better

understanding of the biomechanical forces that cause concussion may lead to more targeted

prevention approaches.



       Although the medical community’s ability to detect, diagnose, and treat SRC has greatly

improved, the ability to prevent SRCs from occurring and decrease the severity of clinical


                                                                           D
outcomes post-injury is limited16. If the acceleration of the brain during an impact can be

decreased14, it has been theorized that this could prevent a concussion from occurring. This is an




                           EP
important concept as the greatest opportunity to impact overall injury burden often lies in injury

prevention14. However, the literature is sparse in regard to concussion prevention in athletes.




                             TE
Patricios et al. has recently published a revised consensus statement on concussion in sport.

While there were five unanimously-supported recommendations for concussion prevention (i:

Mouthguard use should be supported in child and adolescent ice hockey, ii: Policy disallowing

body checking should be supported for all children and most levels of adolescent ice hockey, iii:

Strategies limiting contact practice in American football should inform related policies and

             C
recommendations for all levels, iv: neuromuscular training warm-up programmes are



 C
recommended, based on research in rugby, and more research is needed for female athletes and

in other team sports specifically targeting exercise components aimed to reduce concussion rates,



A
v: Policy supporting optimal concussion management strategies to reduce recurrent concussion

rates is recommended)17, none of the recommendations included cervical strength. Four of the

recommendations were specific to a singular sport and the fifth was a general comment about

policy change17. Thus, there are no agreed upon guidelines or formal recommendations in regard

to cervical strength or cervical strengthening programs and athlete concussion reduction.




                                                        5

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
        Neck size and neck strength have emerged as modifiable characteristics associated with

concussion risk12, 14. Neck size is an easily measured variable given that neck circumference can

be obtained with simple and accessible tools, like a measuring tape. Isometric neck strength,

though a more difficult variable to test due to the need for equipment, such as a dynamometer,

may be more clinically useful because it is a more functional characteristic as opposed to neck

size alone, which is static measurement. There also may be certain athlete populations that could


                                                                           D
benefit from a formal cervical strengthening program, since they have weaker necks18, 19,

including amateur athletes and female athletes. Due to the paucity of research and data on this




                           EP
topic, the purpose of this narrative review is to examine all the literature available regarding neck

size and/or neck strength and its relation to SRC prevention and if a formal cervical strength




                             TE
training program decreases SRCs.



Methods

       A search of Ovid MEDLINE database was performed with the key terms outlined in box

A, resulting in 13 articles. Google Scholar was utilized to search for additional articles with key

             C
terms outlined in box B, resulting in 552 articles. An additional filter to exclude articles prior to



  C
the year 2000 was used, which resulted in 485 articles. As there is a paucity of research in this

area spread across a variety of sports and athlete populations, the inclusion criteria was



A
intentionally kept broad to ensure we captured the literature available on the topic. All articles

relating to sports related concussion and neck size and/or neck strength were included, regardless

of the sport, gender of the athletes, or age of the athletes. The primary author reviewed the

remaining 485 articles and included all 22 articles related to sports related concussion. Two

articles were later removed during the article revision process as they were outside the scope of




                                                        6

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 this manuscript. Combining the 20 articles from Google Scholar and 13 articles from Ovid

MEDLINE resulted in a total of 33 articles included for this literature review (Figure 1).



Discussion

Neck Size

       Neck size, typically measured as neck circumference, was theorized to be a protective


                                                                           D
factor for concussion, as a larger neck could mechanically resist more force and prevent a

concussion from occurring. Neck circumference has been proposed as a simple proxy measure of




                           EP
other features of the cervical spine, such as neck strength20. However, the literature does not

support this theory. Neck circumference has not been shown to be related to SRC history or




                             TE
subsequent SRC. Since neck size is not related to SRC, additional studies examined proportional

neck circumference (neck circumference in proportion to body mass)20. Similarly, there was no

relationship to proportional neck circumference and reduction of SRC. Males had a significantly

larger neck circumference and proportional neck circumference compared to females, but when

controlling for sex, there was no association between neck circumference and SRC20. Eckner et

             C
al. found possible evidence that increased neck size may correlate with reduced concussion risk

in high-school aged male athletes involved in contact or collision sports21. Their results showed

  C
that neck girth, quantified by measuring the circumference of the neck at the level of the thyroid



A
cartilage, was associated with decreased SRC but only with an increase in isometric neck

strength. Collectively, larger neck girth was only associated with decreased SRC if there was

also a concomitant increase in isometric neck strength. There were also findings that an increase

in neck strength without a change in neck girth also led to decreased concussion risk, but the

opposite was not true21. One must be cautious when simply attributing neck circumference to




                                                        7

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 decreased risk of SRC after a cervical strengthening program, as it appears the more pertinent

variable is neck strength. Eckner et al. has suggested a theory that initial strengthening may not

lead to significant changes in neck size, but significant changes in strength. This theory is

consistent with the effect of weight lifting regimes on extremity muscles, where initial strength

gains are from neural adaptation rather than muscle hypertrophy21.



Isometric Neck Strength
                                                                           D
       There is markedly more evidence showing that isometric neck strength is a protective




                           EP
factor from SRC. Cervical musculature is primarily responsible for maintaining posture and

stabilizing the head at rest22. Cervical muscle contraction is theorized to more rigidly couple the




                             TE
head to the torso, and therefore decrease the acceleration experienced by the brain14. Neck

stiffness, via the cervical musculature, is the dynamic ability of the neck to reduce translational

head displacement, velocity, and acceleration15. Individuals who have stronger necks can more

effectively distribute potentially injurious forces from impacts compared to those with weaker

necks23. Greater neck strength has been shown to decrease acceleration of the head during rugby

             C
contact events24. In particular, the sternocleidomastoid muscle has been shown to be the single



 C
muscle making the greatest contribution to force generation across all planes of cervical spine

motion21. Head position at impact can also result in greater forces to the brain. Forward head



A
posture is defined as the external auditory meatus being positioned anterior to the glenohumeral

joint. This particular head position will increase activation of the sternocleidomastoid and upper

trapezius and subsequently inhibit the deep muscles responsible for segmental stability and neck

proprioception. This may result in increased head acceleration during impact due to the muscle

imbalances noted in this posture16.




                                                        8

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
        Not only is strength important, but the symmetry (i.e. balanced strength between neck

flexor and extensor muscle groups) of that strength must be considered. Symmetrical strength in

neck flexors and extensors reduces head acceleration during low-velocity soccer heading in

experienced collegiate players18. Muscle stiffening can allow both the head and torso to absorb

kinetic energy, as opposed to just the head when muscles are not stiffened. This minimizes

acceleration to the head by increasing the relative mass of the head-neck segment since the head


                                                                           D
is better coupled to the torso18, 25. Dezman et al. found that symmetry imbalance in neck

musculature (flexors versus extensors) in the sagittal plane led to higher head accelerations 18, 23.




                           EP
Another way to decrease the acceleration of the head is to extend the time in contact with the ball

(i.e. while heading a soccer ball)18. Acceleration is a result of the speed of an impact per unit of




                             TE
time; therefore, extending the impact over a longer time period will decrease the acceleration of

the head16. Contracted neck muscles are then better able to absorb and dissipate the applied force

on the head down through the neck to the body, thereby minimizing the resultant acceleration of

the head. Additionally, peak linear acceleration was shown to decrease in players who pre-tensed

their neck muscles compared with players who did not25. Collectively, this means that those

             C
soccer players who were able to contract their neck muscles prior to heading a soccer ball had



  C
lower acceleration forces to the head, and thus would be at lower risk of a concussive force.




A      A correlation has been shown between neck strength and head impact kinematics, where

individuals with higher neck strength measurements had lower head accelerations upon impact26.

Imbalances in neck flexor and neck extensor strength ratios in female collegiate soccer athletes

have been correlated with greater angular acceleration when heading the ball. Less overall neck

strength has been significantly correlated with higher concussion rates in basketball, lacrosse,




                                                        9

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 and soccer27. Weaker mean overall neck strength was significantly associated with concussion,

and for every pound of neck strength that athletes gain, their odds of a concussion decreased by

five percent26. There is growing evidence to suggest that neck strength is protective against SRC,

although methods to measure neck strength can be cost prohibitive. For example, in Attwood et

al.’s study the hand held dynamometer used to measure neck strength costs approximately $1000

(US dollars). The associated cost is potentially too expensive for a majority of athletes and/or


                                                                           D
teams, presenting a barrier to access24. In the future, it would be beneficial to develop an

accessible way to measure neck strength, so these measures can be obtained and used across a




                           EP
larger patient population. In addition, if there were standardized values of “at risk” neck strength,

these athletes could be more readily identified. Therefore, we must look toward cervical




                             TE
strengthening programs to determine if they are feasible to carry out and effective at decreasing

SRC. Currently, there is no consensus of whether one type of strengthening program is preferred

over another (i.e. isometric versus eccentric) or if a strengthening program leads to a decrease in

SRC.



             C
Formal Isometric Neck Strengthening Programs



  C    There has been a notable increase in the number of studies assessing whether isometric

cervical strengthening programs can be successfully implemented in athletes to increase their



A
neck musculature in addition to a decrease in SRC. Waring et al. discovered that a six-week

cervical neck strengthening program only improved muscle strength in the anterior and

anterolateral (right and left) directions26. Toninato et al. concluded that greater neck strength was

associated with a decreased kinematic response of the head to controlled impulsive loading28.

Fisher et al. had an eight-week cervical strengthening program where exercises were performed




                                                       10

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 twice per week19. They concluded that there is potential to significantly improve neck strength

using a simple, low volume resistance training protocol19. However, these formal neck

strengthening programs could potentially be an unrealistic regime, as they are commonly

burdensome, require specialist equipment, or a large time commitment, all of which can be

barriers to implementation. Neck muscle function can be altered with targeted resistance training,

but the time and equipment demands are barriers to their implementation24. To combat this issue,


                                                                           D
Attwood et al. performed a study with a under age 18 (U18) male soccer team24. Athletes

performed isometric neck exercises three times per week for eight weeks. These included




                           EP
maximal contraction of the neck in each direction (flexion, extension, left/right lateral flexion)

with resistance provided by their own hands. Total time for exercise was only three minutes and




                             TE
did not require any special equipment. The intervention group’s total neck strength demonstrated

a significant 24% increase over that of the control group. The two major conclusions from the

study were: 1) performing a neck exercise program independently, or as part of a whole-body

program, could contribute to lower sports-related head and neck injuries; and 2) near-maximal to

maximal loads may be required to induce meaningful changes in neck strength when considering

             C
isometric or isotonic neck exercises24. An additional study by Peek at al. reflected the ease with

which a neck strengthening program can be instituted for soccer players25. The rationale for this

 C
study was that players with reduced neck strength often demonstrate an inability to generate the



A
necessary stiffness of the neck column to control the head's response during purposeful heading.

Male and female adolescent soccer players who completed a five-week neuromuscular neck

exercise program integrated into part two of the Federation Internationale de Football

Association’s 11+ Injury Prevention Program (FIFA 11 +) demonstrated an increase in isometric

neck strength and a decrease in head impact magnitude during purposeful heading. Despite




                                                       11

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 adding less than two minutes to part two of the FIFA 11 +, boys and girls in the intervention

group were able to demonstrate large increases in neck strength in only five weeks25. Most

notably, strength increased in neck extensors, with a reported effect size of 0.22 and 95%

confidence interval of (0.08–0.34)25. The conclusion of this study was that players who

completed neck exercises demonstrated an increase in isometric neck strength and a decrease in

head impact magnitude during heading. Importantly, these exercises were easily incorporated


                                                                           D
into the athletes’ usual training. Eckner et al. found that neck strength increased in the

intervention group compared to the control group21. They also concluded that the risk of SRC




                           EP
was significantly reduced with a neck strengthening exercise program. They were also able to

conclude that a five percent decrease in odds of concussion were reported for every one-pound




                             TE
increase in neck strength21. Despite the evidence suggesting the benefits of reduction of SRC

with a simple, efficient, self-performed cervical strengthening program, it does not appear to be a

popular technique implemented by sports teams or athletes. Jeffries et al. discovered that

although nearly 70% of collegiate women’s soccer athletic trainers believed that cervical

strengthening programs would aid in concussion prevention, only 17% currently used such

             C
programs27. Future research could be utilized to determine the optimal exercises, frequency,



  C
duration, and intensity of a cervical strengthening program so that it can be implemented into an

athlete’s training to reduce concussion risk.



A
Non-Professional Athletes’ Cervical Strength

       In regard to concussion prevention, it is important to consider the differences between

professional and amateur athletes because there is conflicting evidence about whether all athletes

would benefit from a cervical strengthening exercise program. There are inherent differences




                                                       12

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 between professional athletes compared to amateur athletes (size, strength, speed, skill, etc). For

instance, Attwood et al. concluded that youth rugby players have significantly lower neck

strength compared with adult rugby players, which may predispose these younger players to

injury, particularly when transitioning to the adult game24. Additionally, there are some physical

attributes that predispose children to concussion. For example, Eckner et al. remarked that

children may be at an even greater disadvantage to sustain a concussion than adults because of


                                                                           D
their greater head mass to body mass ratio15. In a similar study performed by Eckner et al., it was

discovered that a less highly trained youth population training in all three planes of motion might




                           EP
have greater potential for improvement than the elite collegiate athletes21. They found that youth

athletes were able to decrease the rotational accelerations to their head with a cervical




                             TE
strengthening program21. Although no explanation or causation for this finding was provided,

Zasler et al.4 remarks that the incidence rate of SRCs is lower for football at the collegiate level

(4.00 per 10,000 AEs) than the high school level, despite higher injury overall injury rates (e.g.,

orthopedic, musculoskeletal) in collegiate players. Collectively, this highlights how younger

athletes tend to be more at risk for SRC due to certain non-modifiable risk factors. Specifically,

             C
younger athletes may have a greater ability to reduce their concussion risk compared to



  C
professional athletes, since they have relatively weaker necks and, thus, a larger potential to

increase their neck strength.



A      Rotto et al. studied high school football players and determined that a seven-week

cervical strengthening regime prior to the football season led to increased neck strength and

reduced concussions29. The seven-week program was incorporated into the team's pre-season

strength and conditioning workouts. Ultimately, 54 athletes participated in the study; while the




                                                       13

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 team suffered a total of four concussions throughout the season, two of those concussions were

experienced by athletes who did not participate in the strength program. Compared to 12

concussions in the year prior and seven in the season before that, there was a significant

reduction in SRC following the strengthening program29. This study suggests that a cervical

strengthening program can have a direct clinical effect on reducing SRC in athletes, although

larger and more robust trials are needed to strengthen this claim. Hamlin et al. found that a


                                                                           D
simple 6-week neck strengthening program improves maximal voluntary isometric contraction

strength in male amateur rugby players30. The evidence has shown that non-professional athletes




                           EP
tend to have greater risk reduction from concussion when a cervical strength program is

employed.




                             TE
       There is currently a paucity of data describing the relationship between neck strength and

SRC risk, with current research only delineating between professional and non-professional

athletes. More research is needed to fully understand the role of neck strength and SRC in

athletes of all levels, including youth, high school, collegiate, and professional. It has been

             C
suggested that a neck strength assessment could be used as a preparticipation screening for



 C
athletes to identify those who are most at risk for SRC so a strengthening regime can be

proactively implemented into the athlete’s training regimen18.



A
Male versus Female Cervical Strength

       Cervical strengthening programs may result in different outcomes based on the sex of the

athlete. Even the updated consensus statement on concussion admits that more research is needed

for female athletes in regard to concussion prevention17. Prevention strategies may need to be




                                                       14

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 tailored to account for inherent physical characteristics and morphological differences in neck

traits between males and females. For example, the finite element neck model by Braun et al. 31

may provide some insight on these differences. Female vertebrae from C3-7 are significantly

smaller than male vertebrae in the anterior-posterior dimension. Males also have more linear and

areal dimensions of the cervical spine compared to females22. This could indicate males have a

more stable spinal column that could resist inertial loads. Females also have greater ligamentous


                                                                           D
laxity and smaller neck muscles than males22. Ligamentous laxity predisposes a joint to injury as

it is inherently more unstable, and relies more on dynamic stabilizers (i.e. muscles) to prevent




                           EP
injury. A study performed by Carmo et al. examining whiplash injury in motor vehicle collision

showed that females had higher risk of concussion22. Although not sports related, this study




                             TE
suggests that the external forces combined with the female anatomy could lead to differing

exposure to head injury than males. More work is needed to translate the findings of Carmo et al.

to the study of female anatomical characteristics and their role in SRC.



       Gallo et al. has compiled several differences in cervical anatomy and function between

               C
the sexes32. Males had significantly greater peak force and greater time to peak force versus



  C
females for sternocleidomastoid muscles. Males have greater overall cervical muscle strength

compared to females, while females have greater head-neck segment acceleration and



A
displacement than males when exposed to an external force to the head. They also concluded that

there are differences between the sexes in their cervical muscle firing patterns and rates32. Future

cervical strengthening programs may need to consider these factors to tailor programs to males

and females.




                                                       15

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
        The preceding evidence highlights findings in literature to suggest that females

experience SRC more often than males, and they may have a larger reduction in risk if a cervical

strengthening program is implemented. Jeffries et al. concluded that female soccer players have a

concussion incidence rate 2.4 times greater than that of male soccer players, where the majority

of concussions are caused from contact with the ball as opposed to contact with another player27.

The original data came from a case-control study performed by Fuller et al. that included 20


                                                                           D
FIFA tournaments over 6 years resulting in 19,802 player hours of match exposure, which

included 15,115 hours for men and 4,687 hours for women33. They also found that those athletes




                           EP
with weaker neck strength were more likely to suffer concussion, and that females had weaker

necks compared to males27. Peek et al. found similar results whereby female collegiate soccer




                             TE
players exhibited significantly lower neck strength and greater head accelerations during

purposeful heading than males25. In the future, literature will need to address these differences

between the sexes. In order to prevent SRC there may need to be specific exercises tailored

toward males and females. For example, Daly et al. concluded there must be a more

comprehensive understanding of the etiology of concussion in females13 because not only are

             C
females more at risk for SRC, but they report greater symptom severity and longer recovery



 C
times than males. Striefer et al. had similar findings, showing that females experienced more

severe symptoms and longer recovery patterns post-SRC than males16. The fact that females



A
suffer concussion at a greater rate and have more significant symptoms with prolonged recovery

times compared to males highlight the importance of identifying and implementing preventative

measures to offset SRC risk. Although the literature is currently sparse, there is emerging

evidence that neck strengthening exercises can help offset risk of experiencing SRC. Prior work

shows that females achieved greater relative strength increases than males following a




                                                       16

       Copyright © 2024 Wolters Kluwer Health, Inc. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 strengthening regimen, suggesting that the degree of disparity can be reduced19. It has been

hypothesized that females have greater neuromuscular activation to account for their lower neck

strength, which could be one possible mechanism female athletes may rely on for concussion

prevention23. Ultimately, there appears to be a disparity between males and females in regard to

SRC occurrence. This may prove clinically important in the future, as treatment and preventative

measures may also differ between the sexes.



Conclusion and Limitations
                                                                           D
                           EP
       Concussion management has centered around treatment after the injury has occurred, but

it is well known in medicine that injury prevention is the ultimate goal. Primary prevention in




                             TE
regard to SRC is in its infancy, but has some emerging topics. At the forefront is neck or cervical

characteristics, which may serve as protective indicators. However, the evidence to support neck

circumference or size as a protective factor is still lacking. Though an easily measurable trait

with a possibility for a quick screening tool, increased neck size has not yet shown any

relationship to concussion prevention. On the contrary, neck strength does have supportive

             C
evidence to be a protective factor against concussion. More importantly, it has been shown that a



 C
simple neck isometric strengthening program is able to increase neck strength and decrease

concussion risk. However, caution must be exercised as strengthening programs appear to be



A
most helpful in certain populations, like females achieving greater benefit than males, and

amateurs compared to professionals. Similarly, due to the functional and anatomical differences

between the sexes, different exercise programs tailored to sex are needed. It is also unclear if a

cervical strengthening program would benefit athletes in all sports, and the duration, intensity,

and frequency of a cervical strengthening program has yet to be determined.

  "abstract": "Chief medical officers of 15 European professional clubs suggested and rated hamstring injury risk factors. Most were extrinsic, linked to coaching, team or club.   "tldr": "Club medical officers rate communication between medical and coaching staff and high-speed training exposure as the most important hamstring risk factors, and most of the factors they name are controlled by coaching staff. The study shows clinicians' beliefs, not proven causes.",

 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of four newer food supplement categories: pre-workout, fat burner or thermogenic, brain or cognitive booster, and hormone or testosterone booster. The authors report contamination with unauthorized substances, ingredients that are medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA, and conclude that these categories carry the highest risk of harmful ingredients. The review cites survey prevalence data on supplement use in athletes, students and soldiers, but it does not report new outcome data.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search method and no clinical outcome data in athletes. Much of the content is chemical, regulatory and doping-list material, and the ingredient selection was not systematic.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this review as showing that these products harm athletes, when it is a safety and legality review without athlete outcome data.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Jędrejko K, Lazur J, Muszyńska B. Risk Associated with the Use of Selected Ingredients in Food Supplements. Chem Biodivers. 2021;18:e2000686.",
  "doi": "10.1002/cbdv.202000686",
  "abstract": "This review covers four newer categories of food supplements sold in Europe, the US, Australia and parts of Asia. It describes contamination, unauthorized and synthetic ingredients, and WADA-prohibited substances, and it links several ingredients to adverse effects and legal issues. The authors conclude that pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster products have the highest risk of harmful content.",
  "tldr": "Pre-workout, fat burner, brain booster and hormone booster supplements carry the highest risk of harmful or prohibited ingredients. Athletes should check products carefully before use, especially where doping rules apply.",
  "methods": "A narrative review of the chemical, regulatory and doping literature on selected supplement ingredients, with reference to EFSA novel food rules and WADA lists. No systematic search method is described.",
  "findings": "Products in the four categories may contain stimulants, plant ingredients used to disguise stimulants, medicines or synthetic compounds, and substances prohibited by WADA. Some products contain combinations of active ingredients that may cause adverse effects, and some have led to doping sanctions.",
  "limitations": "No systematic search method is described, and the review contains no athlete clinical outcome data. Prevalence figures come from heterogeneous surveys, and product contents vary by brand and batch.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes and staff should check pre-workout, fat burner and hormone-related products against WADA lists and be cautious about unlabelled stimulants. The review supports caution over these categories rather than proof of harm from any single product.",
  "athleteDev": "Athletes using pre-workout or fat-burning supplements should check ingredients against WADA lists and avoid products with undeclared stimulants or hormone-related compounds.",
  "rtp": "Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The review contains no rehabilitation or injury-recovery data."
 }
}

118	
119	Objective: The aim of this systematic review was to identify prospectively measured ankle
120	sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports.
121	Methods: Eight databases including SPORTDiscus, CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE
122	(EBSCO), Education Source, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and Pubmed were searched
123	using specific Boolean terms. A modified-CASP diagnostic test assessed the quality of the
124	included studies. Extensive data extraction included but was not limited to injury definition,
125	protocols for injury diagnosis and recording, and outcomes associated with ankle sprain.
126	Results: 4012 records were returned from the online search and seventeen studies met the
127	inclusion criteria for this review. Twelve different risk factors including anatomic alignment
128	of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI (body mass index), age, ankle strength,
129	hip strength, single leg landing performance (ground reaction force, pelvic internal rotation
130	and knee varus), and single leg reach were all found to be associated with ankle sprain
131	incidence. Injury definitions and methods of diagnosis and recording varied across the 17
132	studies.
133	Conclusion: This review updates the literature on prospective risk factors for ankle sprain in
134	a specific population rather than heterogeneous cohorts previously studied. From more than
135	twenty categories of risk factors investigated for ankle sprain association across seventeen
136	studies in field-based team contact sports, 12 variables were found to be associated with
137	increased incidence of ankle sprain. In order to reduce the risk of ankle sprain, BMI, ankle
138	plantar and dorsiflexion strength, hip strength, and single leg landing performance should be
139	factored in to athlete assessment and subsequent program design. More studies utilizing
140	standardized definitions and methods of recording and reporting are needed. Future
141	prospective etiological studies will allow strength and conditioning coaches, physiotherapists
142	and physicians to apply specific training principles to reduce the risk and occurrence of ankle
143	sprain injuries.

155	                                     1 INTRODUCTION
156	It is widely accepted today that there are multiple physiological, psychological and
157	behavioral benefits to participating in physical activity and sport in most populations [1-11].
158	While the level of benefit varies across populations[12], there is inherent risk associated with
159	participating in physical activity particularly in contact sports [13]. Injuries, particularly to
160	the ankle, have shown an increase in incidence in the last few decades [14] and represent the
161	most frequently injured body location for sports injuries presented to emergency departments
162	in multiple countries [15, 16].
163	
164	The nature of injuries occurring at the ankle include sprains, fractures, dislocations, and
165	ruptures [17]. Sprains have been recorded at two million occurrences per year in the United
166	States, where half (49.3%) are attributed to athletic activities [18]. In sporting populations
167	specifically, ankle sprains are responsible for 15% of all diagnosed injuries [19]. This is the
168	most common injury diagnosed (relative to location and type), in most sports, at different
169	competitive levels, across many countries [15, 19-22]. Furthermore, a study in North
170	American high school athletes investigating costs assessed by quality adjusted life years,
171	discovered that across three years and 648 ankle injuries, of which sprains were most
172	common, there was a mean comprehensive cost of $11,925 per injury [23]. By way of
173	international comparison, data from the Netherlands revealed that, although each ankle sprain
174	was associated with €360 ($507) for direct and indirect cost, their 234,000 incidences per
175	year equated to an estimated €84,240,000 annual expense [24].
176	
177	The ankle complex is organised by two primary sub-joints, the distal tibiofibular which is a
178	fibrous syndesmosis joint, and the talocrural, a uniaxial synovial hinge; each with multiple
179	supporting ligaments [25]. The most common mechanism of injury is ankle inversion and as
180	a result the anterior talofibular ligament has shown to be the most frequently involved
181	ligament in ankle sprains [26, 27]. However, due to the sophistication of this multi-joint
182	complex, damage to a variety of structures can happen with differing associated diagnoses. A
183	sprain injury is defined as structural damage to a ligament. Notably, the three types of ankle
184	sprain are inversion or lateral ankle sprain (LAS), eversion or medial ankle sprain (MAS),
185	and syndesmosis or high ankle sprain (HAS) [28, 29].
186	
187	In addition to the established prevalence, studies investigating several sports have also shown
188	that ligamentous injuries, compared to muscle and tendon (strains), may have the highest
189	severity, that is days lost from participation in training or matches (time-loss) [30, 31]. A
190	recent study investigating injury burden in inline-hockey players representing ten teams and
191	both sexes, found that among all severe injuries (≥29days lost) [32] sprains of the ankle
192	presented the highest prevalence (16%), with ankle fractures second most common (8%).
193	Field-based sports also report high severities from ankle sprain. A recent investigation over
194	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                  4
195	
196	
197	three seasons reported 24.7 average days lost for ankle sprains in rugby union[33], where
198	another study in soccer found an average loss of 33 days for lateral ankle sprains [22].
199	Although many sport settings may lack the resources for regular radiological examination of
200	each ankle injury, a report from the 2016 Summer Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro showed
201	that 10% of all MRIs (magnetic resonance images) performed were at the ankle, of which
202	45% revealed ligamentous injuries [27]. In addition to time-loss, consequences include but
203	are not limited to the direct and indirect costs of diagnosis, treatment and management [34],
204	long-term physical complaints even after 5-years of onset (i.e. chronic ankle instability) [35],
205	and risk of recurrence [36].
206	
207	There has long been a strong focus on injury prevention within the sports science community,
208	first presented in 1992 by Van Mechelen et al. and their four step process [37], and an
209	updated model by Finch in 2006 [38]. In injury epidemiology research and practice, a
210	primary goal is to identify risk factors that may detect early deficits or abnormalities in
211	movement and human performance, which may lead to an increased risk of sustaining injury.
212	These risk factors may pertain to the athlete directly (intrinsic) or their environment
213	(extrinsic). As described by Taimela et al. [39], intrinsic factors (e.g. proprioception) are
214	characteristics which stem from the individual themselves, and predispose oneself to an
215	injury; whereas extrinsic risk factors (e.g. footwear) are independent of the individual but can
216	be related to the onset of injury. Both intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors may be considered
217	modifiable (e.g. strength) or non-modifiable (e.g. leg length) [40]. Extrinsic factors such as
218	playing surface, weather, time zone and travel, have been previously investigated for both
219	risk of injury [41] and player performance [42].
220	
221	Ankle sprains are often reported as the most common injury among athletes, therefore it is
222	necessary for applied practitioners such as strength and conditioning coaches and
223	physiotherapists to know what are the risk factors for ankle injury associated with their
224	particular sport (i.e., field-based, team contact sport [43]). While previous reviews have been
225	conducted regarding ankle sprains, they tend to focus on treatment and management [44-47]
226	or risk of recurrence and long-term effects [48, 49]. For reviews which have identified
227	associated risk factors, some address only one type of ankle sprain [50-52], and others require
228	updating with more recent literature [50, 53]. Therefore, this review aims to fill the gap
229	regarding ankle sprain etiology and update the current literature. Rather than identifying risk
230	factors across many types of sport or physical activity levels [50-54], similar to Ryan et al’s
231	[55] research into groin injury risk factors, this review sought to identify associated risk
232	factors for ankle sprains within field-based, team contact sports.
233	
234	                                          2 METHODS
235	2.1 Literature search methodology
236	The Prisma-P checklist and Explanation and Elaboration was used for reporting [56]. An
237	online search was conducted on eight databases including SPORTDiscus, CINAHL
238	Complete, MEDLINE (EBSCO), Education Source, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and
239	Pubmed with no limitation on publication date.
240	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                    5

243	The following key words and Boolean terms were searched within major topics, titles and
244	abstracts: ‘sport’ AND ‘ankle’ AND [‘injury’ OR ‘sprain’] AND [‘etiolog*’ OR ‘aetiolog*’
245	OR ‘correlat*’ OR ‘risk factor*’ OR ‘susceptib*’ OR ‘associat*’ OR ‘caus*’ OR ‘contribut*’
246	OR ‘predi*’].
247	
248	Studies were eligible for inclusion if they were published in a peer-reviewed academic
249	journal written in English and retrievable as full-text. For full inclusion and exclusion criteria
250	see Table 1. Upon completion of the search strategy by the lead author (PD), duplicates were
251	removed through EndNote X9.3.1 (version 19.2.0.13018). In order to validate the study
252	selection process, two independent reviewers (PD & IK) screened all records found across the
253	eight databases according to the pre-determined list of inclusion and exclusion criteria. Titles
254	and abstracts were initially read, followed by the full-texts. Reference lists of full texts and
255	systematic reviews were screened further to identify any missed prospective studies.

277	2.2 Assessment of Studies and Data Extraction
278	In order to assess the quality of the studies selected for this review, a modification of the
279	Critical Appraisal Skills Programme-Diagnostic Test Study (CASP) [57] was used with some

282	surveillance duration, participant demographics [sex, age, sport and level of competition],
283	exclusion criteria, definition of injury, definition of athletic exposure, type of ankle sprain
284	investigated, injury diagnosis and reporting protocol, baseline physical assessments, and

292	standard deviations (±SD) for injured (INJ) and uninjured (UN) groups were reported, and
293	interpreted as follows (small= 0.2, medium= 0.5, large= .8, very large= 1.3) [59, 60].

296	                                         3 RESULTS
297	3.1 Study selection and characteristics
298	From eight databases, the online search returned 4,012 records, of which 1,291 duplicates
299	were removed. See Figure 1 for PRISMA screening process results. Of the 2,721 remaining,
300	17 papers [61-77] fit the inclusion criteria and were included for review. The characteristics
301	of each study are described in Table 2. Nine different sports were represented in the
302	seventeen studies which included lacrosse [62, 63, 73], soccer [61-68, 70-74], field hockey
303	[62, 63], football (American) [69, 76], Rugby league [75], Rugby union [75], Australian rules
304	football [75], Gaelic football [77], and hurling [77]. The modified CASP assessment is
305	presented in Supplementary Table 1.
306	
307	3.2 Injury surveillance
308	In terms of method of diagnosis, one study confirmed ankle sprains by MRI [75], with eight
309	using assessment by a medical physician [62-64, 66, 68, 72, 74, 77], two using ‘medical staff
310	or personnel’ [67, 71], one using a ‘certified athletic trainer or physician’ [69], and five did
311	not acknowledge confirmation or means of diagnosis [61, 65, 70, 73, 76]. In relation to injury
312	recording, nine studies described their protocol for maintaining injury records [61, 64, 65, 67-
313	70, 75, 76] of which six were maintained by the medical staff as part of the original
314	diagnoses. One study appointed undergraduate students [71], and one had the players
315	themselves maintain their own records [77]. Six studies were unclear in reporting these
316	methods [62, 63, 66, 71, 73, 74]. The incidence rate (no. of sprains / exposure) was not
317	described in ten of the studies [62, 65-69, 71, 72, 76, 77]. From the seven studies that did
318	report overall incidence rate, three studies represented data in (#) sprains/1000 hours:
319	0.6/1000 h [61], 0.36/1000 h [64], 0.47/1000 h [67], 2.16/1000 h [70], and 0.89/1000 h
320	(Rugby union) & 0.46/1000 h (Rugby league) [75]; with one describing in (#) sprains/person-
321	days (p-d), 1.6/1000 p-d (males) & 2.2/1000 p-d (females) [63] and one reported ankle
322	sprains per 10,000 player exposures (12.8 /10,000 AEs) [73].
323	
324	Among the seventeen studies included, four studies did not differentiate between types of
325	sprain (LAS, MAS, HAS) or mechanism of injury (i.e. contact vs non-contact) [61, 65, 66,
326	77]; six investigated inversion sprains only [62-64, 68, 69, 71], while three investigated
327	inversion sprains but excluded contact mechanisms [73, 74, 76]. Additionally, one study
328	investigated only syndesmosis sprains [75]; and two studies reported non-contact mechanism
329	only (no differentiation for type of ankle sprain) [67, 69], of which one reported only LAS in
330	their results [67]. Kofotolis et al. [70] reported ankle sprains by individual ligaments rather
331	than the anatomical region, as well as reported contact and non-contact sprains.

587	3.3 Risk Factors for Ankle Sprain
588	Across the twelve studies, the following categories were investigated: age, sex, injury history,
589	sport, foot/leg dominance, athletic exposure, anthropometrics, general joint laxity, ankle
590	laxity, anatomical alignment, ankle and hip range of motion, ankle strength, calf strength,
591	center of gravity (balance or similar), muscle reaction time (perturbation), hip strength,
592	movement screens, power, body fat%, respiratory capacity, and flexibility.
593	
594	Table 3 presents mass, height, BMI and age as risk factors for ankle sprain from studies that
595	reported these findings. In addition to these anthropometric variables, six studies investigated
596	ankle stability by examining ligamentous laxity [61-63, 66, 67, 73]. The Modified Beighton
597	Method (general laxity) was used in two studies showing no differences between the injured
598	and uninjured groups [62, 63]. Joint laxity of the ankle using the anterior drawer test was
599	used in four studies [61-63, 67], where one study assessed with using an ankle arthrometer
600	and an ankle instability questionnaire [73], again all presenting no statistically significant
601	differences between groups. One study reported a general finding (no method reported) of
602	clinical instability of injured players’ ankles [66]. Arnason et al. [61], Baumhauer et al. [62],
603	and Beynnon et al. [63] also used a second ankle joint laxity test called the Talar Tilt Test,
604	which only Beynnon et al. [63] found a difference between the injured and uninjured groups
605	for males (p= .002), but not in females. These joint laxity tests were dichotomously scored as
606	positive or negative, with no means nor standard deviations reported, and therefore effect size
607	was not calculated.

      Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports:
                                a Systematic Review

Objective: The aim of this systematic review was to identify prospectively measured ankle
sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports.
Methods: Eight databases including SPORTDiscus, CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE
(EBSCO), Education Source, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and Pubmed were searched
using specific Boolean terms. A modified-CASP diagnostic test assessed the quality of the
included studies. Extensive data extraction included but was not limited to injury definition,
protocols for injury diagnosis and recording, and outcomes associated with ankle sprain.
Results: 4012 records were returned from the online search and seventeen studies met the
inclusion criteria for this review. Twelve different risk factors including anatomic alignment
of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI (body mass index), age, ankle strength,
hip strength, single leg landing performance (ground reaction force, pelvic internal rotation
and knee varus), and single leg reach were all found to be associated with ankle sprain
incidence. Injury definitions and methods of diagnosis and recording varied across the 17
studies.
Conclusion: This review updates the literature on prospective risk factors for ankle sprain in
a specific population rather than heterogeneous cohorts previously studied. From more than
twenty categories of risk factors investigated for ankle sprain association across seventeen
studies in field-based team contact sports, 12 variables were found to be associated with
increased incidence of ankle sprain. In order to reduce the risk of ankle sprain, BMI, ankle
plantar and dorsiflexion strength, hip strength, and single leg landing performance should be
factored in to athlete assessment and subsequent program design. More studies utilizing
standardized definitions and methods of recording and reporting are needed. Future
prospective etiological studies will allow strength and conditioning coaches, physiotherapists
and physicians to apply specific training principles to reduce the risk and occurrence of ankle
sprain injuries.




Key Words ankle athletic injuries, athletic performance, epidemiology, etiology, risk factors,
sports, sports medicine, sprains and strains

                                     1 INTRODUCTION
It is widely accepted today that there are multiple physiological, psychological and
behavioral benefits to participating in physical activity and sport in most populations [1-11].
While the level of benefit varies across populations[12], there is inherent risk associated with
participating in physical activity particularly in contact sports [13]. Injuries, particularly to
the ankle, have shown an increase in incidence in the last few decades [14] and represent the
most frequently injured body location for sports injuries presented to emergency departments
in multiple countries [15, 16].

The nature of injuries occurring at the ankle include sprains, fractures, dislocations, and
ruptures [17]. Sprains have been recorded at two million occurrences per year in the United
States, where half (49.3%) are attributed to athletic activities [18]. In sporting populations
specifically, ankle sprains are responsible for 15% of all diagnosed injuries [19]. This is the
most common injury diagnosed (relative to location and type), in most sports, at different
competitive levels, across many countries [15, 19-22]. Furthermore, a study in North
American high school athletes investigating costs assessed by quality adjusted life years,
discovered that across three years and 648 ankle injuries, of which sprains were most
common, there was a mean comprehensive cost of $11,925 per injury [23]. By way of
international comparison, data from the Netherlands revealed that, although each ankle sprain
was associated with €360 ($507) for direct and indirect cost, their 234,000 incidences per
year equated to an estimated €84,240,000 annual expense [24].

The ankle complex is organised by two primary sub-joints, the distal tibiofibular which is a
fibrous syndesmosis joint, and the talocrural, a uniaxial synovial hinge; each with multiple
supporting ligaments [25]. The most common mechanism of injury is ankle inversion and as
a result the anterior talofibular ligament has shown to be the most frequently involved
ligament in ankle sprains [26, 27]. However, due to the sophistication of this multi-joint
complex, damage to a variety of structures can happen with differing associated diagnoses. A
sprain injury is defined as structural damage to a ligament. Notably, the three types of ankle
sprain are inversion or lateral ankle sprain (LAS), eversion or medial ankle sprain (MAS),
and syndesmosis or high ankle sprain (HAS) [28, 29].

In addition to the established prevalence, studies investigating several sports have also shown
that ligamentous injuries, compared to muscle and tendon (strains), may have the highest
severity, that is days lost from participation in training or matches (time-loss) [30, 31]. A
recent study investigating injury burden in inline-hockey players representing ten teams and
both sexes, found that among all severe injuries (≥29days lost) [32] sprains of the ankle
presented the highest prevalence (16%), with ankle fractures second most common (8%).
Field-based sports also report high severities from ankle sprain. A recent investigation over
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                  4


three seasons reported 24.7 average days lost for ankle sprains in rugby union[33], where
another study in soccer found an average loss of 33 days for lateral ankle sprains [22].
Although many sport settings may lack the resources for regular radiological examination of
each ankle injury, a report from the 2016 Summer Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro showed
that 10% of all MRIs (magnetic resonance images) performed were at the ankle, of which
45% revealed ligamentous injuries [27]. In addition to time-loss, consequences include but
are not limited to the direct and indirect costs of diagnosis, treatment and management [34],
long-term physical complaints even after 5-years of onset (i.e. chronic ankle instability) [35],
and risk of recurrence [36].

There has long been a strong focus on injury prevention within the sports science community,
first presented in 1992 by Van Mechelen et al. and their four step process [37], and an
updated model by Finch in 2006 [38]. In injury epidemiology research and practice, a
primary goal is to identify risk factors that may detect early deficits or abnormalities in
movement and human performance, which may lead to an increased risk of sustaining injury.
These risk factors may pertain to the athlete directly (intrinsic) or their environment
(extrinsic). As described by Taimela et al. [39], intrinsic factors (e.g. proprioception) are
characteristics which stem from the individual themselves, and predispose oneself to an
injury; whereas extrinsic risk factors (e.g. footwear) are independent of the individual but can
be related to the onset of injury. Both intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors may be considered
modifiable (e.g. strength) or non-modifiable (e.g. leg length) [40]. Extrinsic factors such as
playing surface, weather, time zone and travel, have been previously investigated for both
risk of injury [41] and player performance [42].

Ankle sprains are often reported as the most common injury among athletes, therefore it is
necessary for applied practitioners such as strength and conditioning coaches and
physiotherapists to know what are the risk factors for ankle injury associated with their
particular sport (i.e., field-based, team contact sport [43]). While previous reviews have been
conducted regarding ankle sprains, they tend to focus on treatment and management [44-47]
or risk of recurrence and long-term effects [48, 49]. For reviews which have identified
associated risk factors, some address only one type of ankle sprain [50-52], and others require
updating with more recent literature [50, 53]. Therefore, this review aims to fill the gap
regarding ankle sprain etiology and update the current literature. Rather than identifying risk
factors across many types of sport or physical activity levels [50-54], similar to Ryan et al’s
[55] research into groin injury risk factors, this review sought to identify associated risk
factors for ankle sprains within field-based, team contact sports.

                                          2 METHODS
2.1 Literature search methodology
The Prisma-P checklist and Explanation and Elaboration was used for reporting [56]. An
online search was conducted on eight databases including SPORTDiscus, CINAHL
Complete, MEDLINE (EBSCO), Education Source, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase and
Pubmed with no limitation on publication date.
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                    5


The following key words and Boolean terms were searched within major topics, titles and
abstracts: ‘sport’ AND ‘ankle’ AND [‘injury’ OR ‘sprain’] AND [‘etiolog*’ OR ‘aetiolog*’
OR ‘correlat*’ OR ‘risk factor*’ OR ‘susceptib*’ OR ‘associat*’ OR ‘caus*’ OR ‘contribut*’
OR ‘predi*’].

Studies were eligible for inclusion if they were published in a peer-reviewed academic
journal written in English and retrievable as full-text. For full inclusion and exclusion criteria
see Table 1. Upon completion of the search strategy by the lead author (PD), duplicates were
removed through EndNote X9.3.1 (version 19.2.0.13018). In order to validate the study
selection process, two independent reviewers (PD & IK) screened all records found across the
eight databases according to the pre-determined list of inclusion and exclusion criteria. Titles
and abstracts were initially read, followed by the full-texts. Reference lists of full texts and
systematic reviews were screened further to identify any missed prospective studies.

2.2 Assessment of Studies and Data Extraction
In order to assess the quality of the studies selected for this review, a modification of the
Critical Appraisal Skills Programme-Diagnostic Test Study (CASP) [57] was used with some
categories sorted or excluded according to the designs of included studies (i.e. sport injury
etiological studies). From the selected studies, the following data were extracted: injury
surveillance duration, participant demographics [sex, age, sport and level of competition],
exclusion criteria, definition of injury, definition of athletic exposure, type of ankle sprain
investigated, injury diagnosis and reporting protocol, baseline physical assessments, and
numerous outcome measures if reported (injury occurrence, athletic exposure, injury rate,
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                  6


ankle sprain grades, number of days missed [severity], and risk association). Tables were
used to present the data according to baseline assessment category in association with ankle
sprain risk. The authors of this review calculated Cohen’s d [58] if the mean values and
standard deviations (±SD) for injured (INJ) and uninjured (UN) groups were reported, and
interpreted as follows (small= 0.2, medium= 0.5, large= .8, very large= 1.3) [59, 60].
Otherwise all data are presented as they were reported in the original studies.

                                         3 RESULTS
3.1 Study selection and characteristics
From eight databases, the online search returned 4,012 records, of which 1,291 duplicates
were removed. See Figure 1 for PRISMA screening process results. Of the 2,721 remaining,
17 papers [61-77] fit the inclusion criteria and were included for review. The characteristics
of each study are described in Table 2. Nine different sports were represented in the
seventeen studies which included lacrosse [62, 63, 73], soccer [61-68, 70-74], field hockey
[62, 63], football (American) [69, 76], Rugby league [75], Rugby union [75], Australian rules
football [75], Gaelic football [77], and hurling [77]. The modified CASP assessment is
presented in Supplementary Table 1.

3.2 Injury surveillance
In terms of method of diagnosis, one study confirmed ankle sprains by MRI [75], with eight
using assessment by a medical physician [62-64, 66, 68, 72, 74, 77], two using ‘medical staff
or personnel’ [67, 71], one using a ‘certified athletic trainer or physician’ [69], and five did
not acknowledge confirmation or means of diagnosis [61, 65, 70, 73, 76]. In relation to injury
recording, nine studies described their protocol for maintaining injury records [61, 64, 65, 67-
70, 75, 76] of which six were maintained by the medical staff as part of the original
diagnoses. One study appointed undergraduate students [71], and one had the players
themselves maintain their own records [77]. Six studies were unclear in reporting these
methods [62, 63, 66, 71, 73, 74]. The incidence rate (no. of sprains / exposure) was not
described in ten of the studies [62, 65-69, 71, 72, 76, 77]. From the seven studies that did
report overall incidence rate, three studies represented data in (#) sprains/1000 hours:
0.6/1000 h [61], 0.36/1000 h [64], 0.47/1000 h [67], 2.16/1000 h [70], and 0.89/1000 h
(Rugby union) & 0.46/1000 h (Rugby league) [75]; with one describing in (#) sprains/person-
days (p-d), 1.6/1000 p-d (males) & 2.2/1000 p-d (females) [63] and one reported ankle
sprains per 10,000 player exposures (12.8 /10,000 AEs) [73].

Among the seventeen studies included, four studies did not differentiate between types of
sprain (LAS, MAS, HAS) or mechanism of injury (i.e. contact vs non-contact) [61, 65, 66,
77]; six investigated inversion sprains only [62-64, 68, 69, 71], while three investigated
inversion sprains but excluded contact mechanisms [73, 74, 76]. Additionally, one study
investigated only syndesmosis sprains [75]; and two studies reported non-contact mechanism
only (no differentiation for type of ankle sprain) [67, 69], of which one reported only LAS in
their results [67]. Kofotolis et al. [70] reported ankle sprains by individual ligaments rather
than the anatomical region, as well as reported contact and non-contact sprains.
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                             7


Four studies investigated the grades of ankle sprains [62, 63, 66, 76], two of which reported
the results [62, 76]. Baumhauer et al. [62] reported 12 Grade-I, 3 Grade-II, and 0 Grade-III
injuries from a total of 15 inversion sprains in their study. Among the 15 diagnosed non-
contact sprains reported by Tyler et al. [76], 11 were Grade-I, 3 were Grade-II, and 1 was a
Grade-III sprain. Severity defined by time-loss was represented in three papers [64, 68, 70].
De Ridder et al. [64] reported an average of moderate severity (8-28 days) per sprain, and a
mean time-loss of 22.4 (±11.7) days, while Fransz et al. [68] reported 17.7 (±11.9, range 3-
54) days for average time-loss, with 32 of the 45 lateral ankle sprains being severe (>7 days
missed). Kofotolis et al. [70] found a mean of 7.01 days lost due to ankle sprains in their
study.
