3.3 Risk Factors for Ankle Sprain
Across the twelve studies, the following categories were investigated: age, sex, injury history,
sport, foot/leg dominance, athletic exposure, anthropometrics, general joint laxity, ankle
laxity, anatomical alignment, ankle and hip range of motion, ankle strength, calf strength,
center of gravity (balance or similar), muscle reaction time (perturbation), hip strength,
movement screens, power, body fat%, respiratory capacity, and flexibility.

Table 3 presents mass, height, BMI and age as risk factors for ankle sprain from studies that
reported these findings. In addition to these anthropometric variables, six studies investigated
ankle stability by examining ligamentous laxity [61-63, 66, 67, 73]. The Modified Beighton
Method (general laxity) was used in two studies showing no differences between the injured
and uninjured groups [62, 63]. Joint laxity of the ankle using the anterior drawer test was
used in four studies [61-63, 67], where one study assessed with using an ankle arthrometer
and an ankle instability questionnaire [73], again all presenting no statistically significant
differences between groups. One study reported a general finding (no method reported) of
clinical instability of injured players’ ankles [66]. Arnason et al. [61], Baumhauer et al. [62],
and Beynnon et al. [63] also used a second ankle joint laxity test called the Talar Tilt Test,
which only Beynnon et al. [63] found a difference between the injured and uninjured groups
for males (p= .002), but not in females. These joint laxity tests were dichotomously scored as
positive or negative, with no means nor standard deviations reported, and therefore effect size
was not calculated.

850	                                        4 DISCUSSION
851	4.1 Summary of Main Findings
852	This study is the first review of ankle sprain risk factors measured in a comprehensive list of
853	field-based, team contact sports. Data from the seventeen studies included in the review came
854	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   19
855	
856	
857	from nine different sports including the sports of lacrosse, soccer, field hockey, American
858	football, rugby league, rugby union, Australian rules football, Gaelic football, and hurling. In
859	total, twenty different categories were assessed as potential risk factors, twelve of which
860	showed an association to ankle sprain incidence [63]. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle
861	strength [62, 67] and hip strength [64, 74], and greater BMI [67, 76] were all associated with
862	an increased likelihood of sustaining an ankle sprain in two different studies each, with single
863	leg landing performance outcomes [68, 73] and single leg anterior reach associated in others
864	[69]. Height [71] and mass [67] were independently associated with ankle sprain risk in other
865	cohorts. Finally, joint laxity was associated with ankle sprain incidence in one study [63]
866	while anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle represented as a risk factor in two different
867	studies [62, 63].
868	
869	4.2 Comparison to Existing Literature
870	Injury events in sport will involve differing kinematics and kinetics thus affecting different
871	anatomical structures [78]. While ankle sprain prevalence across sports has been established,
872	further epidemiological dissection of specific ankle sprain etiology is needed. Varying grades
873	of ankle sprain have previously been defined to aid different treatment strategies [79]. Indeed,
874	diagnosing sprains by grade is one way to categorize severity; but it would prove more
875	beneficial for coaches and medical staff to additionally communicate the impact through
876	estimated time-loss to relevant stakeholders during the course of a season, rather than the
877	architectural state of injured structures [22]. While injury severity (time-loss) is a calculation
878	made retrospectively at the end of a season, only three studies in this review reported average
879	time-loss per ankle sprain [64, 68, 70]. Furthermore, Bahr et al. have suggested there is a
880	need for sport injury epidemiological studies to report injury burden (combining injury
881	severity and incidence rate) to better manage overall risk in the sporting setting [80].
882	
883	4.3 Injury Surveillance
884	For prospectively defining injury, nine studies included time-loss as part of their injury
885	definition, with two studies having required at least a week of absence [74, 77], one required
886	a modified [75] and two required missed [67, 76] game or practice. Two others specified 1
887	day of missed sport activity [69, 71], one at least 48 hours of missed participation [64], and
888	one noted ‘time-loss’ with no specified time window [72]. In order to continue evolving from
889	epidemiological studies to etiological studies, practitioners and researchers should
890	standardize records and reports according to consensus statements published for many sports
891	[81-85], including the most recent consensus statement by the International Olympic
892	Committee [86].
893	
894	4.4 Anthropometric Risk Factors
895	Anthropometric assessments were the most commonly measured category across the
896	seventeen studies. From the ten studies that measured BMI as an independent risk factor,
897	effect sizes varied from medium to large. While De Ridder et al. [64] reported a higher BMI
898	as a significant risk factor with a large effect size, and Fousekis et al. [67] an 8-fold increase
899	in ankle sprain risk for a BMI above the sample median, Watson et al. [77] on the other hand
900	found a negative relationship suggesting that a higher BMI may be protective against ankle
901	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   20
902	
903	
904	sprains. The findings of Watson et al. [77] should be considered with caution as the type of
905	ankle sprains were not reported in their inclusion nor exclusion criteria, and there was a lack
906	of clarity reported in the methods section of this study as evident in CASP assessment. A
907	higher BMI as indicative of risk, similar to the results of De Ridder et al. [64] and Fousekis et
908	al. [67] has also been found previously for general lower extremity injury [87]. It is worth
909	noting that the methods used to measure BMI differed across studies, that is, three studies
910	were vague in their methods of recording mass and height [64, 76, 77], two used a
911	standardized physician scale [67, 71], one did not acknowledge these methods [74], and four
912	utilized self-reporting [62, 63, 69, 75]. This non-invasive recall method does provide a way of
913	saving practitioners time in team settings, while also showing good reliability in recent
914	studies [88], but it would not be considered the gold standard. An additional body size
915	classification (BW x HT2) was investigated originally by Milgrom et al. [89], and found
916	positive association for ankle sprain incidence in military recruits. Similarly, De Ridder et al.
917	[64] showed statistical significance and a large effect size when comparing the injured and
918	uninjured groups in their study. Therefore, further studies are warranted to include this
919	adjusted body size in their methods as a potential risk factor for ankle sprains.
920	
921	4.5 Foot and Ankle Risk Factors
922	Anatomical alignment of the foot and ankle as measured by a goniometer was associated with
923	increased risk of injury in two studies [62, 63]. Dorsiflexion range of motion was considered
924	as a factor for risk in three studies [67, 75, 77], but results were reported in only one [75].
925	Sman et al. [75] used the weight-bearing lunge test which has shown to have ‘good’ inter-
926	and intra-tester reliability, while also showing efficacy for time, space and cost. However,
927	they reported no relationship and a small effect size (Cohen’s d= -.121) between the injured
928	group and uninjured group for dorsiflexion, therefore more evidence is needed to include
929	dorsiflexion as a risk factor. Two [62, 67] of the four [62, 63, 67, 75] studies which measured
930	ankle strength as a risk factor found significant differences between groups. Baumhauer et al.
931	[62] found that between groups, the ratio of concentric eversion:inversion strength was higher
932	in the injured group, and showed a medium effect size (Cohen’s d= 0.52). The same study
933	reported bilateral values within the injured player, finding statistically significant differences
934	but small effect sizes between the injured and uninjured limb in concentric plantarflexion
935	(Cohen’s d= 0.18) and the ratio of concentric dorsiflexion:plantarflexion (Cohen’s d= -.39).
936	Fousekis at al. [67] reported an 8.88 odds ratio for those with a 15% or greater asymmetry in
937	eccentric dorsiflexion and eccentric plantarflexion strength. In an investigation of 241 male
938	physical education students, Willems et al. [90] showed that decreased concentric
939	dorsiflexion strength relative to body mass was also associated with inversion sprains. When
940	ankles are at higher risk due to lack of intrinsic strength or stability [91], many practitioners
941	may argue for the use of external support in prevention of injury for or when returning from
942	injury [92]. However, the only study included in this review to also assess external support as
943	a risk factor [76], showed a significantly higher incidence of 3.9/1,000 athlete-exposures
944	(95% CI, 1.8-7.4) for non-contact inversion sprains for those using tape, braces or both
945	compared to those that did not use any external support 0.5/1,000 athlete-exposures (95% CI,
946	0.2-1.1) (p< .001). Furthermore, a recent meta-analysis has also shown that for patients with
947	history of ankle sprain, external support showed no significant improvement in dynamic
948	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   21
949	
950	
951	postural control for those who did not use support [93], indicating further the importance of
952	decreasing risk of injury onset.
953	
954	4.6 Lower Body Kinematic and Kinetic Risk Factors
955	Three of the eight studies that investigated balance-like traits found significant relationships
956	of moderate to large effect for those who incurred an ankle sprain [68, 69, 73]. Using a force
957	plate, Fransz et al. [68] assessed single leg depth drop landing performance (20 cm height),
958	showing a combined risk factor with stability in the medio-lateral direction within the first
959	0.4 seconds of landing, and stability within the horizontal direction between seconds 3.0 and
960	5.0. As seen in Supplementary Table 2, other independent variables (i.e. peak force vertical,
961	root mean square medio-lateral, mean horizontal late dynamic phase) associated with severe
962	ankle sprains (>1-week time-loss). The second study in this category to show a difference
963	between groups was Gribble et al. [69] using the SEBT (anterior reach) (OR= 2.84), while
964	Sman et al. [75] found no difference in risk of sprain using the SEBT. In 2021 across 167
965	college soccer and lacrosse athletes, Mineta et al. used an eight infra-red camera motion
966	analysis system and forceplate to measure kinetic and kinematic data during single leg
967	landing tasks. They found that when knee varus angle is greater than 0.2º of knee valgus
968	angle there is more than a five-fold increase risk of non-contact LAS, and 24 times greater
969	when pelvic internal rotation is greater than 6º [73]. Neither of the two studies which
970	investigated a modified FMS [69] nor Soccer Injury Movement Screen [72] showed an
971	association with ankle sprains . These mixed results among movement screen scores agree
972	with previously published studies suggesting contradictory findings for general injury
973	association [94, 95]. The inconsistencies across performance tests and methods of statistical
974	analysis throughout this review are particularly evident within this category, inhibiting a
975	collective interpretation across data.
976	
977	4.7 Hip Strength
978	Hip external rotation strength has been considered and demonstrated as a key characteristic
979	for correct landing particularly for mechanics of the knee [96, 97]. De Ridder et al. [64]
980	utilized a hand-held dynamometer to show that decreased posterior hip strength was
981	associated with a greater risk of sustaining a lateral ankle sprain. The second study [74] that
982	tested hip strength found a value of 33.8% of body mass in hip abduction strength was the
983	cut-off for increased risk of sustaining injury. That is to say, for every 1% decrease in relative
984	strength in hip abduction, the risk of injury increases by 10% [74]. When considering the
985	kinetic chain, this evidence warrants further investigation into the role of hip strength and
986	distal ankle sprain injury.
987	
988	4.8 Injury History
989	While this paper reviewed prospective risk factors, many of the included studies also
990	collected questionnaire data regarding athletes’ previous injury, and only two did not [72,
991	77]. Two in fact used previous injury as an exclusion criterion [64, 73]. Baumhauer et al. [62]
992	reported that during their investigation, 27% of those who sustained an ankle sprain had a
993	previous Grade I injury in the same ankle, where Gribble et al. [69] reported 35% had prior
994	ankle sprain history, 75% were recurrent sprains in McCann et al. [71], and Powers et al. [74]
995	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                     22
996	
997	
998	reported 32% of injured had a history of ankle sprain. In addition to reporting previous
999	injuries relative to acquired sprains during the study duration, Sman et al. [75] performed a
1000	Backward Stepwise Cox Regression to find as part of a univariate and multivariate analysis
1001	that previous sprain was not statistically significant for risk. Contradictory to that, Tyler et al.
1002	[76] reported previous ankle sprain as an independent risk factor for future sprain, and when
1003	combining with being overweight (BMI, >95% for age) it resulted in an incidence of 4.27
1004	(95% CI 1.6, 9.3) compared to 0.22 (95% CI .01, 1.2) in normal weighted persons with no
1005	previous injury. Similar to history of ankle sprain as a risk factor, Mineta et al. [73] reported
1006	no group difference in the Identification of Functional Ankle Instability questionnaire scores
1007	between the LAS and non-injured groups. While these historical measures were all
1008	determined through recall, it does identify a risk factor which should be more reliably
1009	measured in future studies. For example, a longitudinal injury surveillance study would have
1010	injury records for each player over the course of several competitive seasons and calendar
1011	years, allowing this risk factor to be measured prospectively with less bias.
1012	
1013	Strengths and Limitations
1014	The current review performed a comprehensive search of eight databases and included
1015	prospective studies which assessed baseline measurements before a competitive season in
1016	field-based team contact sports. By narrowing the search to this population during the
1017	screening process, confounding variables were better controlled for (e.g. sporting rules,
1018	footwear, and surface). Additionally, by utilizing studies with a prospective cohort design,
1019	studies with recall bias were eliminated. There was significant heterogeneity described across
1020	the methods and for the included studies and this inhibited pooled quantitative analyses,
1021	although a recent meta-analysis has taken this approach [51]. Only papers in English were
1022	included in this review. Out of the 17 included studies, only 4 studied women. Other
1023	limitations to this review include not setting an age range for subjects used for inclusion, as
1024	connective tissue (e.g. ligament) maturation may differ between adolescents and adults.
1025	However, if a meta-synthesis was to be performed, they could be excluded in the statistical
1026	analysis, as the distal tibial epiphysis closes between 12 and 15 years of age [98].
1027	
1028	Implications for Practice and Research
1029	From a practical standpoint, even though different sports may have high rates of ankle sprain,
1030	as etiology may vary, coaches need to be able to develop specific programs for their working
1031	population (i.e. needs analysis). For example, if a strength and conditioning coach is
1032	responsible for physical development of a university’s women’s lacrosse and men’s
1033	basketball team, this may be complicated by the fact that these sports result in different types
1034	of sprains, that is, lateral ankle sprains and high ankle sprains, respectively. Without evidence
1035	of associated risk factors for each type of sprain independently, the injury reduction plan for
1036	ankle sprains will likely be a one-model-fits-all approach which may not be appropriate.
1037	
1038	Soccer was the most frequently investigated sport throughout this review, represented in
1039	thirteen of the seventeen studies. Females were only represented in four of the studies. This
1040	suggests a lack of evidence for prospective studies measuring ankle sprain risk factors in
1041	field-based team contact sports and across both sexes. It is worth acknowledging that during
1042	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                  23
1043	
1044	
1045	the screening process, ten papers were excluded for investigating risk factors for general
1046	lower extremity injuries rather than reporting specific location and type (i.e. ankle sprain). A
1047	further five papers did not separate their findings by sport (i.e. population), and the current
1048	authors could not obtain these data from those corresponding authors, thus those papers were
1049	excluded from this review. To date, epidemiological studies have identified the specific
1050	ligaments involved in knee sprains, yet continue to ignore separating types of ankle sprain
1051	(LAS, MAS, HAS) in their reports [32], ignoring the different structures, kinetics, and
1052	mechanisms involved. To progress the impact of applied research, all studies and papers
1053	investigating injury risk factors should adhere to the newly published IOC guidelines for
1054	injury recording and reporting [86]. This standard of practice will aid quantitative
1055	conclusions from level I and level II research [99], identifying which risk factors have highest
1056	sensitivity and specificity for injury risk screening [100].
1057	
1058	When assessing player baseline risk factors, validity and reliability of chosen assessments
1059	need to be considered, with time and cost effectiveness also playing an important role.
1060	Furthermore, all studies included herein used one single assessment period during preseason.
1061	In some cases baseline testing was only performed once while participants were surveyed
1062	across multiple seasons without retesting. In order to increase the validity of the findings,
1063	more research needs to be completed to describe normative changes in these risk factors over
1064	the course of competitive season(s) and determine how often an assessment should be
1065	implemented. Accurate documentation for player attendance in training sessions and matches
1066	will provide more accurate exposure-time and injury incidence rates. When publishing
1067	research, extensive and detailed appendices should be attached for reviewers to access
1068	describing means (±SD) for injured and uninjured groups, confidence intervals, as well as
1069	providing data separated by sex, sport type, and playing position. As previously suggested,
1070	when consensus statements are not able to be followed, studies should describe which
1071	resources were limited in their design that prevented them from doing so [85].
1072	
1073	Many challenges to conducting prospective etiological research in sports injuries have been
1074	laid out previously by Bahr [100]. His paper identifies appropriate and successive steps to
1075	validate a screening test, yet indicates that no such test has been appropriately justified to
1076	predict sporting injuries. This support, along with the important quantitative limitations from
1077	this review into ankle sprain risk factors, reinforce that practitioners should design
1078	interventions around injury incidence frequencies rather than potential risk of causative
1079	factors. Furthermore, specific programs which target multiple body parts should be
1080	considered, as sports elicit many injury types across various bodily locations.
1081	
1082	                                     5 CONCLUSIONS
1083	This review has two overall findings, firstly from more than twenty categories of risk factors
1084	investigated for ankle sprain association across seventeen studies in field-based team contact
1085	sports, 12 variables were found to be associated with increased incidence of ankle sprain in
1086	field-based team contact sport athletes. From the studies reviewed, no movement screen
1087	scores including from a modified-FMS nor Soccer Injury Movement Screen showed an
1088	increased risk of sustaining ankle sprain. In order to reduce the risk of ankle sprain, practical
1089	 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                        24
1090	
1091	
1092	assessment of BMI, ankle plantar and dorsiflexion strength, hip strength, and single leg
1093	landing performance should be factored in to athlete assessment and subsequent program
1094	design. Ankle sprain interventions must be included in a whole-body program in order to
1095	maximize the transfer from research to pragmatically reducing injuries. In addition to these
1096	practitioner focused elements, considering that ankle sprains are the most prevalent injury
1097	across all sports, from this review it remains clear that more prospective studies with large
1098	sample sizes across both sexes, utilizing standardized definitions and methods of recording
1099	and reporting are needed. While etiological studies will identify risk factors, there will always
1100	be an inherent risk of injury in sport. Therefore, applied research will intend to reduce injury
1101	risk, occurrence or severity, rather than prevent.

Two studies used hand-dynamometers to measure isometric hip strength in relation to ankle
sprain risk [64, 74], and both data sets are presented in Table 5. Two studies investigated
power as a potential risk factor. Sman et al. [75] used a vertical counter-movement jump with
arm swing by way of either a VertecTM or jump testing mat, where those with ankle sprain
(n=12) jumped 63.6 (±8.20) cm during baseline testing compared to those without sprain who
achieved 59.10 (±7.8) cm (p= .05) (Cohen’s d= .577). Arnason et al. [61] investigated ankle
sprain association to a squat test, a countermovement jump, and a standing jump to which no
differences between injured and non-injured groups were found. Body fat %, respiratory
capacity, and flexibility were investigated by Arnason et al. [61] and Watson et al. [77] but
only one stated no significant association to ankle sprain where the other [77] referred to
them in their methods but were not reported in the study’s results. Risk factors described by
authors as center of gravity, balance, proprioception, postural sway or movement screens are
compiled to one category (kinematics and kinetics) for representation in Supplementary
Table 2 [63, 67-69, 72, 73, 75, 77].

                                        4 DISCUSSION
4.1 Summary of Main Findings
This study is the first review of ankle sprain risk factors measured in a comprehensive list of
field-based, team contact sports. Data from the seventeen studies included in the review came
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   19


from nine different sports including the sports of lacrosse, soccer, field hockey, American
football, rugby league, rugby union, Australian rules football, Gaelic football, and hurling. In
total, twenty different categories were assessed as potential risk factors, twelve of which
showed an association to ankle sprain incidence [63]. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle
strength [62, 67] and hip strength [64, 74], and greater BMI [67, 76] were all associated with
an increased likelihood of sustaining an ankle sprain in two different studies each, with single
leg landing performance outcomes [68, 73] and single leg anterior reach associated in others
[69]. Height [71] and mass [67] were independently associated with ankle sprain risk in other
cohorts. Finally, joint laxity was associated with ankle sprain incidence in one study [63]
while anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle represented as a risk factor in two different
studies [62, 63].

4.2 Comparison to Existing Literature
Injury events in sport will involve differing kinematics and kinetics thus affecting different
anatomical structures [78]. While ankle sprain prevalence across sports has been established,
further epidemiological dissection of specific ankle sprain etiology is needed. Varying grades
of ankle sprain have previously been defined to aid different treatment strategies [79]. Indeed,
diagnosing sprains by grade is one way to categorize severity; but it would prove more
beneficial for coaches and medical staff to additionally communicate the impact through
estimated time-loss to relevant stakeholders during the course of a season, rather than the
architectural state of injured structures [22]. While injury severity (time-loss) is a calculation
made retrospectively at the end of a season, only three studies in this review reported average
time-loss per ankle sprain [64, 68, 70]. Furthermore, Bahr et al. have suggested there is a
need for sport injury epidemiological studies to report injury burden (combining injury
severity and incidence rate) to better manage overall risk in the sporting setting [80].

4.3 Injury Surveillance
For prospectively defining injury, nine studies included time-loss as part of their injury
definition, with two studies having required at least a week of absence [74, 77], one required
a modified [75] and two required missed [67, 76] game or practice. Two others specified 1
day of missed sport activity [69, 71], one at least 48 hours of missed participation [64], and
one noted ‘time-loss’ with no specified time window [72]. In order to continue evolving from
epidemiological studies to etiological studies, practitioners and researchers should
standardize records and reports according to consensus statements published for many sports
[81-85], including the most recent consensus statement by the International Olympic
Committee [86].

4.4 Anthropometric Risk Factors
Anthropometric assessments were the most commonly measured category across the
seventeen studies. From the ten studies that measured BMI as an independent risk factor,
effect sizes varied from medium to large. While De Ridder et al. [64] reported a higher BMI
as a significant risk factor with a large effect size, and Fousekis et al. [67] an 8-fold increase
in ankle sprain risk for a BMI above the sample median, Watson et al. [77] on the other hand
found a negative relationship suggesting that a higher BMI may be protective against ankle
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   20


sprains. The findings of Watson et al. [77] should be considered with caution as the type of
ankle sprains were not reported in their inclusion nor exclusion criteria, and there was a lack
of clarity reported in the methods section of this study as evident in CASP assessment. A
higher BMI as indicative of risk, similar to the results of De Ridder et al. [64] and Fousekis et
al. [67] has also been found previously for general lower extremity injury [87]. It is worth
noting that the methods used to measure BMI differed across studies, that is, three studies
were vague in their methods of recording mass and height [64, 76, 77], two used a
standardized physician scale [67, 71], one did not acknowledge these methods [74], and four
utilized self-reporting [62, 63, 69, 75]. This non-invasive recall method does provide a way of
saving practitioners time in team settings, while also showing good reliability in recent
studies [88], but it would not be considered the gold standard. An additional body size
classification (BW x HT2) was investigated originally by Milgrom et al. [89], and found
positive association for ankle sprain incidence in military recruits. Similarly, De Ridder et al.
[64] showed statistical significance and a large effect size when comparing the injured and
uninjured groups in their study. Therefore, further studies are warranted to include this
adjusted body size in their methods as a potential risk factor for ankle sprains.

4.5 Foot and Ankle Risk Factors
Anatomical alignment of the foot and ankle as measured by a goniometer was associated with
increased risk of injury in two studies [62, 63]. Dorsiflexion range of motion was considered
as a factor for risk in three studies [67, 75, 77], but results were reported in only one [75].
Sman et al. [75] used the weight-bearing lunge test which has shown to have ‘good’ inter-
and intra-tester reliability, while also showing efficacy for time, space and cost. However,
they reported no relationship and a small effect size (Cohen’s d= -.121) between the injured
group and uninjured group for dorsiflexion, therefore more evidence is needed to include
dorsiflexion as a risk factor. Two [62, 67] of the four [62, 63, 67, 75] studies which measured
ankle strength as a risk factor found significant differences between groups. Baumhauer et al.
[62] found that between groups, the ratio of concentric eversion:inversion strength was higher
in the injured group, and showed a medium effect size (Cohen’s d= 0.52). The same study
reported bilateral values within the injured player, finding statistically significant differences
but small effect sizes between the injured and uninjured limb in concentric plantarflexion
(Cohen’s d= 0.18) and the ratio of concentric dorsiflexion:plantarflexion (Cohen’s d= -.39).
Fousekis at al. [67] reported an 8.88 odds ratio for those with a 15% or greater asymmetry in
eccentric dorsiflexion and eccentric plantarflexion strength. In an investigation of 241 male
physical education students, Willems et al. [90] showed that decreased concentric
dorsiflexion strength relative to body mass was also associated with inversion sprains. When
ankles are at higher risk due to lack of intrinsic strength or stability [91], many practitioners
may argue for the use of external support in prevention of injury for or when returning from
injury [92]. However, the only study included in this review to also assess external support as
a risk factor [76], showed a significantly higher incidence of 3.9/1,000 athlete-exposures
(95% CI, 1.8-7.4) for non-contact inversion sprains for those using tape, braces or both
compared to those that did not use any external support 0.5/1,000 athlete-exposures (95% CI,
0.2-1.1) (p< .001). Furthermore, a recent meta-analysis has also shown that for patients with
history of ankle sprain, external support showed no significant improvement in dynamic
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                   21


postural control for those who did not use support [93], indicating further the importance of
decreasing risk of injury onset.

4.6 Lower Body Kinematic and Kinetic Risk Factors
Three of the eight studies that investigated balance-like traits found significant relationships
of moderate to large effect for those who incurred an ankle sprain [68, 69, 73]. Using a force
plate, Fransz et al. [68] assessed single leg depth drop landing performance (20 cm height),
showing a combined risk factor with stability in the medio-lateral direction within the first
0.4 seconds of landing, and stability within the horizontal direction between seconds 3.0 and
5.0. As seen in Supplementary Table 2, other independent variables (i.e. peak force vertical,
root mean square medio-lateral, mean horizontal late dynamic phase) associated with severe
ankle sprains (>1-week time-loss). The second study in this category to show a difference
between groups was Gribble et al. [69] using the SEBT (anterior reach) (OR= 2.84), while
Sman et al. [75] found no difference in risk of sprain using the SEBT. In 2021 across 167
college soccer and lacrosse athletes, Mineta et al. used an eight infra-red camera motion
analysis system and forceplate to measure kinetic and kinematic data during single leg
landing tasks. They found that when knee varus angle is greater than 0.2º of knee valgus
angle there is more than a five-fold increase risk of non-contact LAS, and 24 times greater
when pelvic internal rotation is greater than 6º [73]. Neither of the two studies which
investigated a modified FMS [69] nor Soccer Injury Movement Screen [72] showed an
association with ankle sprains . These mixed results among movement screen scores agree
with previously published studies suggesting contradictory findings for general injury
association [94, 95]. The inconsistencies across performance tests and methods of statistical
analysis throughout this review are particularly evident within this category, inhibiting a
collective interpretation across data.

4.7 Hip Strength
Hip external rotation strength has been considered and demonstrated as a key characteristic
for correct landing particularly for mechanics of the knee [96, 97]. De Ridder et al. [64]
utilized a hand-held dynamometer to show that decreased posterior hip strength was
associated with a greater risk of sustaining a lateral ankle sprain. The second study [74] that
tested hip strength found a value of 33.8% of body mass in hip abduction strength was the
cut-off for increased risk of sustaining injury. That is to say, for every 1% decrease in relative
strength in hip abduction, the risk of injury increases by 10% [74]. When considering the
kinetic chain, this evidence warrants further investigation into the role of hip strength and
distal ankle sprain injury.

4.8 Injury History
While this paper reviewed prospective risk factors, many of the included studies also
collected questionnaire data regarding athletes’ previous injury, and only two did not [72,
77]. Two in fact used previous injury as an exclusion criterion [64, 73]. Baumhauer et al. [62]
reported that during their investigation, 27% of those who sustained an ankle sprain had a
previous Grade I injury in the same ankle, where Gribble et al. [69] reported 35% had prior
ankle sprain history, 75% were recurrent sprains in McCann et al. [71], and Powers et al. [74]
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                     22


reported 32% of injured had a history of ankle sprain. In addition to reporting previous
injuries relative to acquired sprains during the study duration, Sman et al. [75] performed a
Backward Stepwise Cox Regression to find as part of a univariate and multivariate analysis
that previous sprain was not statistically significant for risk. Contradictory to that, Tyler et al.
[76] reported previous ankle sprain as an independent risk factor for future sprain, and when
combining with being overweight (BMI, >95% for age) it resulted in an incidence of 4.27
(95% CI 1.6, 9.3) compared to 0.22 (95% CI .01, 1.2) in normal weighted persons with no
previous injury. Similar to history of ankle sprain as a risk factor, Mineta et al. [73] reported
no group difference in the Identification of Functional Ankle Instability questionnaire scores
between the LAS and non-injured groups. While these historical measures were all
determined through recall, it does identify a risk factor which should be more reliably
measured in future studies. For example, a longitudinal injury surveillance study would have
injury records for each player over the course of several competitive seasons and calendar
years, allowing this risk factor to be measured prospectively with less bias.

Strengths and Limitations
The current review performed a comprehensive search of eight databases and included
prospective studies which assessed baseline measurements before a competitive season in
field-based team contact sports. By narrowing the search to this population during the
screening process, confounding variables were better controlled for (e.g. sporting rules,
footwear, and surface). Additionally, by utilizing studies with a prospective cohort design,
studies with recall bias were eliminated. There was significant heterogeneity described across
the methods and for the included studies and this inhibited pooled quantitative analyses,
although a recent meta-analysis has taken this approach [51]. Only papers in English were
included in this review. Out of the 17 included studies, only 4 studied women. Other
limitations to this review include not setting an age range for subjects used for inclusion, as
connective tissue (e.g. ligament) maturation may differ between adolescents and adults.
However, if a meta-synthesis was to be performed, they could be excluded in the statistical
analysis, as the distal tibial epiphysis closes between 12 and 15 years of age [98].

Implications for Practice and Research
From a practical standpoint, even though different sports may have high rates of ankle sprain,
as etiology may vary, coaches need to be able to develop specific programs for their working
population (i.e. needs analysis). For example, if a strength and conditioning coach is
responsible for physical development of a university’s women’s lacrosse and men’s
basketball team, this may be complicated by the fact that these sports result in different types
of sprains, that is, lateral ankle sprains and high ankle sprains, respectively. Without evidence
of associated risk factors for each type of sprain independently, the injury reduction plan for
ankle sprains will likely be a one-model-fits-all approach which may not be appropriate.

Soccer was the most frequently investigated sport throughout this review, represented in
thirteen of the seventeen studies. Females were only represented in four of the studies. This
suggests a lack of evidence for prospective studies measuring ankle sprain risk factors in
field-based team contact sports and across both sexes. It is worth acknowledging that during
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                  23


the screening process, ten papers were excluded for investigating risk factors for general
lower extremity injuries rather than reporting specific location and type (i.e. ankle sprain). A
further five papers did not separate their findings by sport (i.e. population), and the current
authors could not obtain these data from those corresponding authors, thus those papers were
excluded from this review. To date, epidemiological studies have identified the specific
ligaments involved in knee sprains, yet continue to ignore separating types of ankle sprain
(LAS, MAS, HAS) in their reports [32], ignoring the different structures, kinetics, and
mechanisms involved. To progress the impact of applied research, all studies and papers
investigating injury risk factors should adhere to the newly published IOC guidelines for
injury recording and reporting [86]. This standard of practice will aid quantitative
conclusions from level I and level II research [99], identifying which risk factors have highest
sensitivity and specificity for injury risk screening [100].

When assessing player baseline risk factors, validity and reliability of chosen assessments
need to be considered, with time and cost effectiveness also playing an important role.
Furthermore, all studies included herein used one single assessment period during preseason.
In some cases baseline testing was only performed once while participants were surveyed
across multiple seasons without retesting. In order to increase the validity of the findings,
more research needs to be completed to describe normative changes in these risk factors over
the course of competitive season(s) and determine how often an assessment should be
implemented. Accurate documentation for player attendance in training sessions and matches
will provide more accurate exposure-time and injury incidence rates. When publishing
research, extensive and detailed appendices should be attached for reviewers to access
describing means (±SD) for injured and uninjured groups, confidence intervals, as well as
providing data separated by sex, sport type, and playing position. As previously suggested,
when consensus statements are not able to be followed, studies should describe which
resources were limited in their design that prevented them from doing so [85].

Many challenges to conducting prospective etiological research in sports injuries have been
laid out previously by Bahr [100]. His paper identifies appropriate and successive steps to
validate a screening test, yet indicates that no such test has been appropriately justified to
predict sporting injuries. This support, along with the important quantitative limitations from
this review into ankle sprain risk factors, reinforce that practitioners should design
interventions around injury incidence frequencies rather than potential risk of causative
factors. Furthermore, specific programs which target multiple body parts should be
considered, as sports elicit many injury types across various bodily locations.

                                     5 CONCLUSIONS
This review has two overall findings, firstly from more than twenty categories of risk factors
investigated for ankle sprain association across seventeen studies in field-based team contact
sports, 12 variables were found to be associated with increased incidence of ankle sprain in
field-based team contact sport athletes. From the studies reviewed, no movement screen
scores including from a modified-FMS nor Soccer Injury Movement Screen showed an
increased risk of sustaining ankle sprain. In order to reduce the risk of ankle sprain, practical
 Ankle Sprain Risk Factors in Field-Based Team Contact Sports                                        24


assessment of BMI, ankle plantar and dorsiflexion strength, hip strength, and single leg
landing performance should be factored in to athlete assessment and subsequent program
design. Ankle sprain interventions must be included in a whole-body program in order to
maximize the transfer from research to pragmatically reducing injuries. In addition to these
practitioner focused elements, considering that ankle sprains are the most prevalent injury
across all sports, from this review it remains clear that more prospective studies with large
sample sizes across both sexes, utilizing standardized definitions and methods of recording
and reporting are needed. While etiological studies will identify risk factors, there will always
be an inherent risk of injury in sport. Therefore, applied research will intend to reduce injury
risk, occurrence or severity, rather than prevent.

Declarations
Ethics All procedures set out in this paper have been approved by the relevant institution’s
ethics committee

Disclosure of interest All authors declare no conflict of interest that are relevant to the
content of this review.

Availability of Data The original datasets analyzed from included studies during the current
review are available from the corresponding author upon request.

2.     McMahon, E.M., et al., Physical activity in European adolescents and associations with
       anxiety, depression and well-being. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry, 2017. 26(1): p. 111-122.
3.     Sun, F., I.J. Norman, and A.E. While, Physical activity in older people: a systematic review.
       BMC public health, 2013. 13(1): p. 449.

        a

    This review focuses on four new product categories of food supplements: pre-workout, fat burner/
thermogenic, brain/cognitive booster, and hormone/testosterone booster. Many food supplements have been
shown to be contaminated with unauthorized substances. In some cases, the ingredients in the new categories
of dietary supplements were medicinal products or new synthetic compounds added without performing clinical
trials. Some of the new ingredients in dietary supplements are plant materials that are registered in the
pharmacopoeia as herbal medicines. In other cases, dietary supplements may contain plant materials that have
no history of human use and are often used as materials to ‘camouflage’ stimulants. In the European Union, new
ingredients of dietary supplements, according to European Food Safety Authority or unauthorized novel food.
Furthermore, selected ingredients in dietary supplements may be prohibited in sports and are recognized as
doping agents by World Anti-Doping Agency.

Keywords: doping, food supplements, new components, SARM, steroids, stimulants, toxicology.

16	Abstract
17	Background Causes of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are multifactorial. Anterior cruciate ligament injury pre-
18	vention should thus be approached from a multifactorial perspective as well. Training to resist fatigue is an underestimated
19	aspect of prevention programs given that the presence of fatigue may play a crucial role in sustaining an ACL injury.
20	Objectives The primary objective of this literature review was to summarize research findings relating to the kinematic and
21	kinetic effects of fatigue on single-leg landing tasks through a systematic review and meta-analysis. Other objectives were to
22	critically appraise current approaches to examine the effects of fatigue together with elucidating and proposing an optimized
23	approach for measuring the role of fatigue in ACL injury prevention.
24	Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in the databases PubMed (1978–November 2017), CINAHL (1992–
25	November 2017), and EMBASE (1973–November 2017). The inclusion criteria were: (1) full text, (2) published in English,
26	German, or Dutch, (3) healthy subjects, (4) average age ≥ 18 years, (5) single-leg jump landing task, (6) evaluation of the
27	kinematics and/or kinetics of the lower extremities before and after a fatigue protocol, and (7) presentation of numerical
28	kinematic and/or kinetic data. Participants included healthy subjects who underwent a fatigue protocol and in whom the
29	effects of pre- and post-fatigue on three-dimensional lower extremity kinematic and kinetics were compared. Methods of
30	data collection, patient selection, blinding, prevention of verification bias, and study design were independently assessed.
31	Results Twenty studies were included, in which four types of single-leg tasks were examined: the single-leg drop vertical
32	jump, the single-leg drop landing, the single-leg hop for distance, and sidestep cutting. Fatigue seemed to mostly affect
33	initial contact (decreased angles post-fatigue) and peak (increased angles post-fatigue) hip and knee flexion. Sagittal plane
34	variables at initial contact were mostly affected under the single-leg hop for distance and sidestep cutting conditions whilst
35	peak angles were affected during the single-leg drop jump.
36	Conclusions Training to resist fatigue is an underestimated aspect of prevention programs given that the presence of fatigue
37	may play a crucial role in sustaining an ACL injury. Considering the small number of variables affected after fatigue, the
38	question arises whether the same fatigue pathways are affected by the fatigue protocols used in the included laboratory stud-
39	ies as are experienced on the sports field.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



Revised Approach to the Role of Fatigue in Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Injury Prevention: A Systematic Review with Meta‑Analyses
Anne Benjaminse1,2          · Kate E. Webster3 · Alexander Kimp3 · Michelle Meijer4 · Alli Gokeler5,6


© The Author(s) 2019


Abstract
Background Causes of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are multifactorial. Anterior cruciate ligament injury pre-
vention should thus be approached from a multifactorial perspective as well. Training to resist fatigue is an underestimated
aspect of prevention programs given that the presence of fatigue may play a crucial role in sustaining an ACL injury.
Objectives The primary objective of this literature review was to summarize research findings relating to the kinematic and
kinetic effects of fatigue on single-leg landing tasks through a systematic review and meta-analysis. Other objectives were to
critically appraise current approaches to examine the effects of fatigue together with elucidating and proposing an optimized
approach for measuring the role of fatigue in ACL injury prevention.
Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in the databases PubMed (1978–November 2017), CINAHL (1992–
November 2017), and EMBASE (1973–November 2017). The inclusion criteria were: (1) full text, (2) published in English,
German, or Dutch, (3) healthy subjects, (4) average age ≥ 18 years, (5) single-leg jump landing task, (6) evaluation of the
kinematics and/or kinetics of the lower extremities before and after a fatigue protocol, and (7) presentation of numerical
kinematic and/or kinetic data. Participants included healthy subjects who underwent a fatigue protocol and in whom the
effects of pre- and post-fatigue on three-dimensional lower extremity kinematic and kinetics were compared. Methods of
data collection, patient selection, blinding, prevention of verification bias, and study design were independently assessed.
Results Twenty studies were included, in which four types of single-leg tasks were examined: the single-leg drop vertical
jump, the single-leg drop landing, the single-leg hop for distance, and sidestep cutting. Fatigue seemed to mostly affect
initial contact (decreased angles post-fatigue) and peak (increased angles post-fatigue) hip and knee flexion. Sagittal plane
variables at initial contact were mostly affected under the single-leg hop for distance and sidestep cutting conditions whilst
peak angles were affected during the single-leg drop jump.
Conclusions Training to resist fatigue is an underestimated aspect of prevention programs given that the presence of fatigue
may play a crucial role in sustaining an ACL injury. Considering the small number of variables affected after fatigue, the
question arises whether the same fatigue pathways are affected by the fatigue protocols used in the included laboratory stud-
ies as are experienced on the sports field.

                                                                        Key Points

                                                                        Current fatigue protocols might over-simplify a complex
                                                                        system.
                                                                        An optimized approach to the role of fatigue in anterior
                                                                        cruciate ligament injury prevention might be necessary
                                                                        in which workload, aerobic fitness and fatigue serve as
                                                                        interacting factors.

{
 "id": "Q05",
 "sourceFile": "Risk and prognosis of hamstring injuries in the National Football League - A 12-year review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Rehabilitation"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "American Football"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Injured Athletes"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Descriptive epidemiology study of weekly NFL injury report listings for hamstring injuries over 12 seasons from the public NFL database. It identified 2101 hamstring injuries in 1354 players, and 442 players (33%) had at least one reinjury. Mean time on the injury report was 2.4 weeks, and time on the report for reinjuries did not differ significantly from initial injuries (2.4 vs 2.2 weeks, P = .138).",
 "screeningLimitations": "Public injury-report data omit preseason injuries, tear severity, imaging and treatment, and cover elite players only, so results may not transfer to lower levels. Team injury rates are shares of listings rather than exposure-adjusted, and the descriptive design cannot show causes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the team-to-team injury-rate differences (0.6% to 5.7% of listings) as evidence that some organizations' prevention or treatment works, when the data cannot show exposure, programs or causes.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Jenkins R, Bianchi J, Watson J, Shinners J, Jaisinghani P, Spain B, et al. Risk and Prognosis of Hamstring Injuries in the National Football League: A 12-Year Review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024;12(12):23259671241298622.",
  "doi": "10.1177/23259671241298622",
  "abstract": "This descriptive study used public NFL injury report data to examine hamstring injuries over 12 seasons. About one third of players were reinjured, and team-level injury rates varied widely. The authors suggest further research into why preventive measures and treatment protocols differ between organizations.",
  "tldr": "NFL hamstring injuries kept players on the injury report about 2.4 weeks on average, and about one third of injured players were reinjured. Staff should plan for reinjury risk, but this database cannot explain why some teams have more injuries.",
  "methods": "Weekly NFL injury report listings for hamstring injuries were extracted from the public NFL database for 12 seasons. Time on the injury report, practice and game status, position, team rates and reinjury were summarized with descriptive statistics, t tests and chi-square tests.",
  "findings": "There were 2101 hamstring injuries in 1354 players, and 442 players (33%) had a reinjury. Defensive skill players accounted for 50.4% of listings, and linebackers had the highest share at 20.1%. Previous injury was not associated with a longer time on the injury report.",
  "limitations": "Only in-season listings were used, preseason injuries are not in the database, and tear severity, imaging and treatment are not reported. Data come from elite players with dedicated rehabilitation staff. The overall mean time on the report is given as 2.4 weeks, while the initial-injury value in the reinjury comparison is 2.2 weeks.",
  "practicalImplications": "Expect a substantial share of players with a hamstring injury to be reinjured, and build reinjury monitoring into rehabilitation and return-to-play planning. Team-level differences should prompt a review of prevention and treatment practices rather than be taken as proof of what works.",
  "athleteDev": "Skill-position players, especially linebackers, wide receivers and cornerbacks, made up most hamstring listings, so they are a priority group for tracking hamstring injury history. The study does not test any prevention program.",
  "rtp": "The average time on the injury report was 2.4 weeks, and previous injury was not linked to a longer absence. The study does not test return-to-play criteria or show that any return timing reduces reinjury, so it should not set return timelines on its own."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "evidenceSummary: 'reinjuries were not longer than first injuries' -> no significant difference ('No significant difference was observed in duration on the IR for reinjury compared with initial injury (2.4 ± 1.8 vs 2.2 ± 1.7 weeks; P = .138)')",
   "paper.findings: 'injuries' -> 'listings' for position shares, which are computed from the 4812 weekly listings (Table 1, defensive skill 2426 (50.4))",
   "paper.limitations: added the 2.4 vs 2.2 week inconsistency for initial injury duration ('The mean number of consecutive weeks on the IR for a hamstring injury was 2.4 ± 2.1 weeks')",
   "paper.athleteDev: removed unsupported advice on change-of-direction exposure planning and record keeping -> position finding only ('LBs were most likely to be injured, making up 20.1%, followed by WR at 19.9% and CB at 18.7%')"
  ],
  "residualConcerns": "The paper reports reinjury duration 2.4 vs initial 2.2 weeks, but the overall mean was also 2.4 weeks, so which value belongs to which group is unclear in the source. The conclusion says 'more than a third' reinjured while the count is 442 of 1354 (33%).",
  "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

 "sourceFile": "Risk factors for acute ankle sprains in field-based, team contact sports - A systematic review of prospective etiological studies.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Training & Performance"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Athletic Training",
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Performance"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport",
  "Soccer",
  "American Football",
  "Rugby",
  "Other Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Healthy Athletes",
  "Male Athletes",
  "Female Athletes",
  "Professional / Elite",
  "Collegiate",
  "Youth / Adolescent",
  "Adult / Recreational"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Systematic review of 17 prospective studies across nine field-based team contact sports, from 4,012 records found in eight databases. The authors report that 12 of 20 risk-factor categories were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including ankle strength, hip strength, BMI, height, mass, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach. Most of these associations came from only one or two studies, and injury definitions and diagnosis methods varied widely.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The pooled evidence rests on 17 studies with inconsistent injury definitions, diagnosis methods and incidence reporting, and only seven reported an incidence rate. Several associations come from single studies, and the BMI findings conflict, with one study reporting a protective effect.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the 12 associated factors as validated screening tests for ankle sprain, when most rest on one or two studies that used different definitions.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Dolan P, Kenny I, Glynn L, Campbell M, Warrington GD, Cahalan R, et al. Risk Factors for Acute Ankle Sprains in Field-Based, Team Contact Sports: a Systematic Review of Prospective Etiological Studies. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1080/00913847.2022.2093618",
  "abstract": "This systematic review identified prospectively measured ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Seventeen studies met the criteria, and 12 risk-factor categories were associated with ankle sprain incidence. The authors suggest that BMI, ankle strength, hip strength and single-leg landing performance be considered in athlete assessment, and call for standardized injury definitions.",
  "tldr": "Ankle strength, hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance were linked to ankle sprain risk across team sports, but the evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use these measures in screening with awareness of the limits, and record injuries with standard definitions.",
  "methods": "Eight databases were searched for prospective studies of ankle sprain risk factors in field-based team contact sports. Study quality was rated with a modified CASP checklist, and data were extracted from the 17 included studies.",
  "findings": "Twelve risk factors were associated with ankle sprain incidence, including anatomic alignment of the foot and ankle, joint laxity, height, mass, BMI, age, ankle strength, hip strength, single-leg landing performance and single-leg reach. Deficits or asymmetries in ankle strength and hip strength were each associated in two studies.",
  "limitations": "Only the accepted author version was available, so pagination is missing. Injury definitions and diagnosis varied, only seven of 17 studies reported an incidence rate, and only four studied women. Several associations come from single studies, and the BMI findings conflict across studies.",
  "practicalImplications": "Ankle and hip strength, BMI and single-leg landing performance can be included in athlete assessment as the authors suggest, with the thin evidence base in mind. Measuring these in a standardized way across seasons would make results more useful.",
  "athleteDev": "Use ankle and hip strength tests and single-leg landing and reach screening as part of athlete assessment and program design, as the review proposes. Record injuries with standard definitions so findings can be checked locally.",
  "rtp": "The review concerns the risk of ankle sprain measured from preseason baselines. It does not inform return-to-play decisions after an ankle sprain."
 },
 "verification": {
  "status": "CORRECTED",
  "changes": [
   "populations: added Adult / Recreational for amateur and lower-division samples ('North division soccer league of the Greek Amateur Association'; '5th Division soccer')",
   "paper.limitations: added that only 4 of 17 studies included women ('Out of the 17 included studies, only 4 studied women')",

  ],

  "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}
